vcs-5792:
The Togo Green Renaissance with Farmers and Schools Project (the “Project”) is an Agriculture, Forestry and Other Land Use (AFOLU) initiative implemented in Togo, West Africa, using the Verra VM0047 methodology. Developed by Reboisement et Exploitation des Forêts SARL (REF), the Project addresses land degradation, deforestation, and climate vulnerability while strengthening rural livelihoods and environmental education.

Togo has experienced severe deforestation, with forest cover declining to approximately 7% of total land area by 2010 due to unsustainable agricultural practices, population pressure, and fuelwood dependence. These pressures have led to widespread land degradation, soil erosion, and declining productivity. The Project responds through large-scale, community-driven reforestation and agroforestry implemented as a grouped project over an 8–10-year period.

Activities are implemented nationwide across REF-managed lands, smallholder farms, and educational institutions, primarily on degraded or low-tree-cover lands with limited natural regeneration. The Project comprises three components: approximately 8% (2,000 ha) REF-managed mixed-species reforestation, 56% (14,000 ha) farmer-led agroforestry involving over 1,500 farmers (with 377,800 trees planted across 158.83 ha to date), and 36% (9,000 ha) school-based greening interventions across more than 3,000 schools.

Overall, the Project targets over 63 million trees and is expected to generate greenhouse gas removals primarily through biomass accumulation. It intends to generate VCUs under the Verra VCS and pursue CCB certification, with ex-ante projections estimating average removals of ~1.5 million tCO₂e per year and total removals of ~27 million tCO₂e over the crediting period, subject to verification.
vcs-5795:
The PrithviPoshan Biochar Project is a large-scale carbon sequestration initiative focused on converting cow dung into biochar to address rising greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and improve agricultural sustainability. The feedstock is sourced from a partner organization Shri Godham Mahateerth Pathmeda Lok Punyarth Nyas, a Non-Governmental Organization that operates a network of cow shelters (gaushalas) with over 150,000 cattle. The project utilizes a high-tech pyrolysis facility capable of processing 100 tonnes of manure daily to produce approximately 14,600 dry metric tonnes of biochar annually. The system is a continuous rotary system where pyrolysis gases are scrubbed and utilized to heat the pyrolytic chamber and the excess gas combusted in a thermal oxidizer with waste heat recovery, thus avoiding methane emissions. Excess heat from the thermal oxidizer is utilized to dry and preheat the feedstock before it enters the pyrolysis chamber. The feedstock will be pyrolyzed at an optimized temperature of 550℃, which exceeds the World Biochar Certificate (WBC) requirement of 500℃ for 3 minutes for animal manure, ensuring the elimination of biological hazards and micropollutants. Automated metering and an IOT-enabled interface are used to log production parameters such as feedstock input, biochar output, and pyrolysis chamber temperature, ensuring tamper-proof data for verification. The produced biochar undergoes rigorous quality assurance, with samples tested for moisture, organic carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) to ensure permanence and compliance with standards like a molar H/Corg ratio less than 0.7. 
This is a grouped project with facilities located in India. The first project activity /instance (the Nandgaon facility) is located in the Vadvaj Village, District Sirohi, Rajasthan. The biochar plant is strategically located within the premises of the Shree Manorama Golok Teerth - Nandgaon gaushala (source of waste generation) to minimize transport-related emissions. The project will use bullock carts to transport waste from various pens within the gaushala to the production facility.
The primary mechanism is the conversion of waste cow manure into biochar, a stable form of carbon. This process directly reduces methane emissions that would otherwise be released from decomposing manure. The biochar produced is a long-term carbon sink, enhancing soil health and providing carbon sequestration benefits when applied to agricultural land. The project specifically ensures non-combustive use of biochar as a soil amendment. 
The Nandgaon facility alone is estimated to remove 18,415 tCO2e of GHG emissions from the atmosphere annually for a total of 1,28,908 tCO2e over the first crediting period i.e. 1 July 2026 to 30th June 2033.
vcs-5798: The project is an improved forest management initiative that transforms logging activities into forest conservation efforts. vcs-5799:
The Gerbang Barito REDD+ Project Area consists of two Village Forests, Batampang Village Forest and Batilap Village Forest in Central Kalimantan, Indonesia. The 19,752 ha Project Area is administratively part of the Central Kalimantan province which oversees the Village Forests. It is located within the Gerbang Barito Forest Management Unit and is in the geographic range of the critically endangered Bornean orangutan. The Village Forests that make up the Project Area are part of the traditional Dayak lands where most of the residents are Dayak tribes who live along the Barito River and rely on the Village Forests for their livelihoods.

The Project Area is under threat from unplanned deforestation and peat decomposition. The key drivers of deforestation in the Project Area are illegal logging, bird hunting, construction of drainage canals, and unsustainable fishing practices. Drained peatland from existing canals and reduced forest cover from deforestation are the primary drivers of peat decomposition in the Project Area. 

The lowland forest of Central Kalimantan is one of the biodiversity-rich plains on Kalimantan Island. Wildlife Works has identified four High Conservation Values within the Project Area. These include: (1) Species Diversity, including endemic and non-endemic threatened endangered species, (2) Ecosystem and Habitats, representing rare, threatened or endangered ecosystems, habitats or refugia, (3) Ecosystem services, including protection of water catchments and control of erosion of vulnerable soils and slopes, and (4) Basic needs of communities, such as water supply, fisheries, transportation, timber, and non-timber forest products.

Village Forests are regulated by the Ministry of Forestry under the “Social Forestry” scheme for Indigenous Peoples and Local Communities. The communities of Batampang and Batilap are entitled to manage their Village Forests and consequently they are the carbon rights owners.

The Suledo Forest is a crucial ecosystem and a lifeline for 13 Indigenous villages that depend on it for water, food, grazing, and cultural identity for Maasai communities. Decades of pressure have left large areas degraded, threatening both community livelihoods and biodiversity. The Suledo Project aims to restore this forest through community-led action, combining active planting with assisted natural regeneration (ANR). The communities will lead the restoration and conservation of the forest. The project is designed not only to restore the landscape but also to build local knowledge, enabling communities to earn their livelihoods through restoration and conservation rather than forest degradation. A benefit-sharing plan is in place to actively develop forest-supporting activities that align with traditional communal lifestyles, ensuring long-term engagement and thereby strengthening the project’s permanence.

Over its lifetime, the project targets the restoration of 10,000 hectares, designed to remove an estimated 2.45 million tonnes of CO₂. Beyond carbon, it will secure biodiversity habitats, safeguard watersheds, and enhance soil fertility. What sets Suledo apart is its deep community ownership. The villages themselves govern and protect the forest under a community-led trust. Restoration activities will also generate alternative livelihoods, including honey, dairy, and sustainable land use practices, reducing pressure on natural forests and strengthening household incomes.
vcs-5803: This project will take place on cropland in the Moyamba District of Sierra Leone, on lands of the Kamajei Chiefdom. All the involved cropland is managed and leased by Leone Agriculture Ltd, and is owned by Kamajei Chiefdom, whose Paramount Chief (PC) is PC Fayia Sundifu Brima Sovula IV. The project will begin with 15,000 acres of cropland and this could scale up over the duration of the project. The purpose of this project will be primarily to increase carbon sequestration in soils and woody biomass, while increasing the productivity of the involved cropland. The project area will introduce the following interventions to meet these goals: improving agroforestry through the planting of apple-ring trees (Faidherbia albida) with intercropping of previously grown crops. This project will utilize the VCS Methodology VM0042 (Version 2.2), Methodology for Improved Agricultural Land Management. This project will use VM0042’s Quantification Approach 2: Measure and Re-Measure. Soil sampling will be used to measure soil organic carbon, and above and below ground woody biomass will be measured using Verra’s recommended CDM A/R tools.
vcs-5805:
Mangrove forests are like natural walls that protect the coast. They stop the shoreline from washing away, reduce damage from storms, and help against rising sea levels. They are also a crucial home for many different aquatic animals. On top of that, mangroves are excellent at absorbing and storing large amounts of carbon, which helps in the fight against climate change.The project actively enhances carbon sequestration by establishing mangrove plantations that absorb atmospheric carbon dioxide through photosynthesis. The accumulated carbon is stored both in the aboveground biomass and within the soil matrix, thereby contributing to climate change mitigation.
The project Climeverse Private Limited dba Equilibrium. They are working with a local partner and the people who live in the area.The site is currently a tidal wetland with or without patches of grasses (Dhani Grass - Porteresia coarctata).This project will establish new mangrove forests on 4,000 hectares of intertidal mudflats in India, specifically within the Sundarbans region (North and South 24 Parganas, West Bengal) and Odisha. The first implementation phase will target 500 hectares of the total 2,000-hectare area in West Bengal.
Species selection is conducted using site-specific ecological assessments, integrating scientific knowledge and community insights. A diverse assemblage of mangrove species, including Avicennia officinalis, Avicennia alba, Bruguiera gymnorhiza, Ceriops decandra and Heritiera littoralis, is being established to promote ecological resilience and long-term carbon storage potential. 

Over a 40-year crediting period, it is projected to remove a total of 2,022,125 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (tCO₂e), with an annual average removal of approximately 50,553 tCO₂e for the 2,000-hectare area. This project follows the strict rules of the VCS-approved VM0033 Methodology for Tidal Wetland and Seagrass Restoration, v2.1 to make sure these calculations are accurate.
vcs-5806: Tausi Forests Limited, a joint venture between Shell Nature Based Solutions (Shell NBS) and the New Forests Company (NFC), will implement a carbon project in the Southern Highlands of Tanzania. vcs-5807:
The Regenerative Agriculture Carbon Offsetting Program (RACO) is a grouped project with New Energy Centre Malaysia Sdn. Bhd (NECM) as the project proponent. This grouped project aims to assist farmers in Malaysia, particularly low - income and small - holder farmers, in adopting improved cropland management and regenerative agricultural practices on their own farms. 
Over time, some agricultural lands in Malaysia have undergone a certain degree of degradation due to anthropogenic factors, environmental conditions, and extreme weather events. Agriculture plays a crucial role in supporting the country's food security as well as the health and welfare of its people. Malaysia has a mainly tropical rainforest climate and tropical monsoon climate. Although precipitation is relatively abundant, it is unevenly distributed. Moreover, affected by climate change, extreme rainfall and drought events occur from time to time, which accelerates soil degradation, significantly reduces soil organic matter, and further decreases soil productivity, thus constraining agricultural productivity and stability. Meanwhile, in pursuit of agricultural output, some farmers have carried out unreasonable agricultural activities, such as excessive deep tillage and over-fertilization, to make up for the decline in land productivity, which has aggravated soil degradation and damaged the farm ecosystem.
In this scenario, the RACO project provides a significant opportunity to improve the croplands in the region and restore soil organic matter by providing eligible farmers with microalgae as a substitute for synthetic fertilizer. This initiative not only enables carbon removal but also enhances overall soil health.
The grouped project encompasses a series of improved cropland management practices, including reducing tillage depth, adding microalgae as soil amendment, minimizing the use of synthetic fertilizers, applying organic fertilizers, integrating pest management, improving irrigation system

vcs-5815: The Bronkhorstspruit Biogas Plant sources organic waste stream from the surrounding local area and produces biogas which is used for green energy generation using an anaerobic digester. vcs-5816: The Massangui Forest Conservation and Afforestation Project combines the protection of existing forests with the establishment of new tree cover to restore degraded landscapes in the Bouenza department of the Republic of the Congo. vcs-5817:
SAJOMA Climate Technical Consulting S.A.S. de C.V. (hereafter SAJOMA Climate Technical Consulting, or SAJOMA) is developing a sustainable grouped project (GP) of biogas recovery and utilization to generate thermal energy, improving treatment systems for animal waste generated by livestock farms in Mexico. The proposed technology of the grouped project includes anaerobic biodigesters to treat animal waste.   
The project activity aims to install high-efficiency anaerobic digester systems (e.g. HDPE Membrane Enclosed Anaerobic Digester), equipped with a flare, and (when applicable) biogas utilization equipment (e.g. filters to reduce humidity and Sulphur content) to allow the use of the biogas as a renewable fuel to generate thermal energy at steam boilers (e.g. retrofitted/new) substituting fossil fuels. 
Depending on the specific conditions at each site, the project activity instances may include the installation of reception tanks to homogenize the substrate waste and to separate the solids before entering into the biodigester, and other pumping equipment to ensure proper operation of the technology.  
Under the baseline scenario, farms’ waste is treated under conventional methods, including open anaerobic lagoons, which release methane-rich biogas directly into the atmosphere. The proposed technology allows to reduce the greenhouse gases (GHG) emissions by capturing methane emissions that would have been otherwise emitted, and by displacing the consumption of fossil fuels. In some cases, farms within the grouped project might employ biogas for electricity generation; however, emission reductions will not be claimed for this component. The estimated GHG emission reductions annual average per project activity instance will be less than 60,000 tCO2e, which is the small-scale threshold as defined for the project Type III for waste management.
vcs-5818:
The Avé Ga Project (“Big Forest” in Ewe) is a large-scale, community-based reforestation and agroforestry (ARR) initiative aiming to restore 15,750 ha of degraded community and public lands in Togo, West Africa. The project enhances climate resilience and ecosystem restoration by establishing diversified agroforestry systems and woodlots adapted to local socio-ecological conditions. Farmers transition from low-diversity cash crop systems (e.g., beans, cassava, cotton) to mixed agroforestry models that integrate fruit, fertilizer, and timber trees, including perennial crops such as coffee, cocoa, and cashew. These systems build on over 20 years of successful local experience, modernizing ancestral African practices to ensure productivity, long-term cultivation, and natural regeneration.

Beyond tree planting, nursery development, and Farmer-Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR), the project strengthens community resilience through wildfire prevention training, cooperative development, and participatory rural planning. Local committees and herder groups guide livelihood and infrastructure initiatives, ensuring inclusiveness and ownership.

The implementation approach rests on four strategic pillars: (1) Enhancing carbon stocks and biodiversity through reforestation and regeneration; (2) Restoring resilient and diversified agricultural systems via mixed-species agroforestry; (3) Strengthening community governance for sustainable rural development; (4) Structuring value chains for perennial crops to improve market access, food security, and local economies.

Addressing degradation from slash-and-burn farming and unregulated logging, the project stabilizes soils, restores fertility, and halts deforestation. Over its 40-year longevity period, it is expected to sequester 6.2 million tCO₂, averaging 174,000 tCO₂e carbon removals per year, while fostering climate-resilient livelihoods and community-driven ecosystem restoration.
vcs-582: The main objective of the Yaylabel HPP is to generate electricity from renewable energy sources that provides to the Turkish National Power Grid with an installed capacity of 5.2 MW, consisting of 2 vertical axis pelton turbines (2*2,600 kW) with an estimated power generation 20.43 GWh in each year. The Project is expected to reduce CO2 emissions by an estimated 11,094 tonnes CO2 annually.
vcs-5820: The Gamboma and Mbon Afforestation Project focuses on creating new forest cover in the Nkéni-Alima and Plateaux Departments of the Republic of the Congo. vcs-5821: The proposed ARR project aims to restore degraded and fallow agricultural landscapes across selected regions of Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh through large-scale community-based tree planting. The project will establish approximately 6 million mixed native and agroforestry tree species on privately owned farmlands, including fallow plots, degraded lands, and field bunds. By increasing tree cover outside traditional forest areas, the project seeks to enhance ecological resilience, improve soil health, and sequester atmospheric carbon over the 20-year crediting period. The project is implemented through a participatory approach that ensures full involvement of local farmers, marginalized groups, and tribal communities. In addition, the project integrates robust monitoring systems through a digital MRV platform using high-resolution satellite imagery, geo-tagged field data, and survival-tracking tools. Mixed native species, including timber, fruit, fodder, and multipurpose trees, are selected based on agro-climatic suitability and farmer preference. No natural ecosystems are disturbed, and project activities avoid protected areas, ensuring full compliance with VCS and national regulations.
vcs-5822: The Mwenga Hydro Power Project is a 3.486 MWe micro-scale run-of-river hydro power plant on the Mwenga River located in Mufindi District of the Iringa Region in Southern Tanzania. Started generation to the grid on 21 September 2012
vcs-5823:
The “FORÊTS D’AVENIR” Grouped Project is a large-scale ecosystem restoration initiative focused on restoring degraded drylands at risk of desertification. The project aims to restore over 25,000 hectares of degraded land in Senegal through community-based reforestation and sustainable land management practices, with an annual planned expansion of at least 1,500 hectares. Activities are designed to deliver long-term carbon removals, enhance biodiversity, regenerate ecosystem services, and support climate-resilient livelihoods in vulnerable rural areas.
The project uses a silvo-pastoral reforestation approach adapted to semi-arid and degraded conditions. Native tree species are directly seeded on degraded land; species establishment is aided through ground preparation using the Delfino Vallerani plough. Livestock exclusion is ensured through fencing, and long-term land stewardship is formalised through the creation of Community Forest Management Committees (CFMCs), which engage local communities in site selection, seed sourcing, species choice, and ongoing management. Species are selected based on ecological, cultural, and economic value, including nitrogen-fixing, medicinal, fruit-bearing, and high-value native timber trees. 
The FORÊTS D’AVENIR project is structured as a grouped initiative, enabling the inclusion of additional project activity instances over time. Consequently, the project area covers all of Senegal, including every degraded land category within the “Domaine National” and the “Domaine Public de l’État”. In addition to the climate benefits, the project delivers benefits in biodiversity conservation, water retention, erosion control, soil health and the revitalisation of rural economies. It contributes to improved local governance through CFMCs and fosters inclusive decision-making and forest-based value chains.
vcs-5826:
This project utilizes waste CO₂ (otherwise emitted to the atmosphere) or atmospheric CO₂ as a feedstock in concrete production. It reduces greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions through two core mechanisms:
1.CO₂ Mineralization: CO₂ is permanently sequestered in concrete during manufacturing;
2.Cement Reduction: The process requires less Portland cement—whose production is highly energy- and carbon-intensive—further cutting emissions.
The project is implemented at precast concrete manufacturing sites (where cement, water, aggregates, etc., are mixed). Specifically:Shenzhen Carbonminer Technology (Group) Co., Ltd. provides carbon curing equipment to Guangzhou Development Environmental Protection Building Materials Co., Ltd. for producing autoclaved aerated concrete blocks (GDG blocks). Compared to conventional concrete production lines (without carbon curing equipment), the upgraded line is projected to produce 50,000 cubic meters (m³) of GDG blocks annually while sequestering 5,000 tonnes (t) of CO₂ per year.
The project aims to generate VCS carbon credits by achieving GHG reductions/removals, in compliance with the VM0043 Methodology (Version 1.1). During the monitoring period (01 August 2024 – 31 April 2025), total GHG emission reductions reached 23 tCO₂eq.
vcs-5827: The Scaw Electric Arc Furnace Efficiency Project, located in Gauteng South Africa, involves the installation and operation of a power feeder system aiming to improve the operational efficiency of the Electric Arc Furnace. This Project reduces GHG emissions by reducing the amount of coal-based electricity consumption from South Africa’s national grid.
vcs-583: Yazi Hydro-Electric Power Plant targets to supply about 1.13 MW of renewable electricity to the rapidly grow Turkish electricity market. The project is expected to generate about 5.203 MWh of electricity annually and to reduce 2,825 tonnes of CO2 emissions per year.
vcs-5831:
The Igarapé Lourdes REDD+ Project is a community-led initiative to reduce unplanned deforestation and forest degradation through conservation and sustainable land management, guided by the Territorial and Environmental Management Plan (PGTA). The PGTA ensures activities align with community priorities, cultural values, and governance structures. Core actions include forest protection, ethnozoning, participatory land-use planning, and capacity-building programs to strengthen local governance and resilience.
The project is implemented through a partnership among the Igarapé Lourdes community associations—ZAVDIDJAJ DJIGUHR (ASSIZA), KARO PAYGAP, MA’PÁYRAP KARORAP, and MAPÃY PAYÚ KARO—with technical support from Centro de Estudos Rioterra, a non-profit promoting sustainable development in the Amazon. A financial mechanism, AICA REDD, was established to ensure transparency and manage resource distribution under terms authorized by the indigenous associations.
The project area spans 196,014 hectares within the Igarapé Lourdes Indigenous Territory (IT), located in Ji-Paraná, Rondônia, along the border with Mato Grosso. It includes riverine floodplains, terra firme forests, and seasonally inundated grasslands. The territory is home to the Karo Arara, Ikolen Gavião, and isolated Serra da Previdência groups, whose deep spiritual and subsistence ties to waterways, forests, and ancestral hunting grounds guide project priorities.
By preventing forest loss and promoting biodiversity conservation, the project reduces greenhouse gas emissions, particularly CO₂. Before implementation, the territory faced threats from illegal logging, land encroachment, and limited institutional capacity, endangering ecosystems and cultural integrity.
Expected impact: an average annual reduction of 52,416 tCO₂e, totaling 2,096,625 tCO₂e over 40 years—demonstrating its significant contribution to climate mitigation in addition to community and biodiversity co-benefits.
vcs-5832:
O Projeto REDD+ ZORÓ PANGYJEJ é uma iniciativa comunitária voltada para reduzir o desmatamento não planejado e a degradação florestal por meio de práticas integradas de conservação e gestão sustentável da terra, guiadas pela revisão e implementação do Plano de Gestão Territorial e Ambiental (PGTA). A PGTA serve como uma estrutura estratégica para o planejamento e execução de atividades, garantindo alinhamento com as prioridades da comunidade, valores culturais e estruturas de governança. As atividades centrais do projeto incluem proteção florestal, etnozoneamento, planejamento participativo do uso do solo e programas de capacitação projetados para fortalecer a governança local e aumentar a resiliência.
O projeto é implementado pela associação representativa do povo Zoró, APIZ (Associação Indígena do Povo Zoró – PANGYEJ), com apoio técnico do Centro de Estudos Rioterra, uma organização sem fins lucrativos comprometida em promover modelos de desenvolvimento sustentável na região amazônica. Para garantir transparência e responsabilidade, foi criado um mecanismo financeiro dedicado — AICA REDD — para gerenciar a distribuição de recursos de acordo com os termos autorizados pela associação indígena.
Localizado dentro do Território Indígena (IT) Zoró em Rondolândia, Mato Grosso, Brasil, a área do projeto abrange 355.789 hectares no bioma amazônico. Este território é lar do povo Zoró Pangyjej, cuja conexão cultural e espiritual com a floresta molda as prioridades do projeto. 
Ao prevenir a perda de florestas e promover a conservação da biodiversidade, o projeto reduz significativamente as emissões de gases de efeito estufa, especialmente dióxido de carbono. Antes da implementação, o território enfrentava graves ameaças de corte ilegal, invasão de terras e capacidade institucional limitada, colocando em risco tanto o ecossistema florestal quanto a integridade cultural do povo Zoró.
Por meio dessas intervenções, espera-se que o projeto alcance uma redução média anual de aproximadamente 241.477 tCO₂e, totalizando cerca de 9.659.076 tCO₂e ao longo do período de crédito de 40 anos.
vcs-5833: The bundled project activity involves the controlled aerobic decomposition of the biodegradable organic fraction of Municipal Solid Waste (MSW) through windrow composting across three urban locations named Siliguri, Pramod Nagar, and Varanasi. The combined waste processing capacity is 1,397 tonnes per day (TPD). The project is implemented and operated by Eastern Organic Fertilizer Private Limited (EOFPL) with the objective of avoiding methane emissions that would otherwise arise from the uncontrolled anaerobic decomposition of MSW in open landfill sites.
vcs-5834:
The Delta Kapuas Project area is located in West Kalimantan Province and comprises of 25 village forests, covering a total area of approximately 122,119.88 Ha. This region has met the requirements for emission reduction activities that will be implemented in the area as Reduced Emission of Deforestation and Degradation (REDD), Afforestation Reforestation and Rehabilitation (ARR) as well as Wetland Restoration and Conservation (WRC). The project area encompasses 3 (three) main ecosystem types in the area namely mineral soil, wetlands, and mangroves. These ecosystem types are spread across 25 village forest areas within West Kalimantan Province covering approximately 122,119.88 Ha.

The objectives of this project are based on three key aspects: climate, community and biodiversity. From a climate perspective, the project aims to reduce GHG (Greenhouse Gas) emissions from deforestation and forest degradation by protecting forest areas within the project region, enhancing the institutional capacity of LPHD, and restoring mangrove and wetland ecosystems. From a community perspective, the project aims to improve the well-being of local community by strengthening local governance and increasing community awareness of the value of forests conservation and sustainable resource management. From a biodiversity perspective, the project aims to protect natural habitats within the project area that support endemic and protected species such as Orangutan Kalimantan (Pongo pygmaeus), Bekantan (Nasalis larvatus), Trenggiling (Manis javanica), Owa Janggut-putih (Hylobates albibarbis), Rangkong Badak (Buceros rhinoceros), Julang Jambul-hitam (Rhabdotorrhinus corrugatus), Kura-kura Matahari (Heosemys spinosa), Ramin (Gonystylus bancanus), Meranti Lilin (Shorea teysmanniana), and Tumu putih (Bruguiera hainesii).
vcs-5836: Defending Rainforest at the Highest-Deforestation Frontlines from Otherwise-Certain Destruction: The project conducts defensive interventions (through active monitoring and community and other interventions) at the Highest-Deforestation Frontline, with the goal of stopping deforestation and related carbon release, biodiversity loss, freshwater loss and community conflict. Targeted interventions are deployed to safeguard these rainforest areas, ensuring the preservation of intact forest cover in regions most vulnerable to active and high deforestation pressures.
vcs-5837: Restoring Rainforest and its full Biodiversity at the Highest-Deforestation Frontlines: The XARR Grouped Project conducts restorative interventions (through active and passive re-seeding and planting along the Highest-Deforestation Frontline, with the goal of restoring already-destroyed areas to its full biodiversity (and ultimately, to step deforestation of nearby and adjacent rainforest areas). Targeted interventions are deployed to restore critical areas initially along the active treeline, and to gradually restore further already-destroyed areas. Restorative interventions under the XARR Grouped Project will be conducted through nature-assisted restoration using only local seeds, and a combination of local indigenous and science-based restoration techniques.
vcs-5838:
Rio Branco REDD+ Project is a community-driven initiative aimed at reducing unplanned deforestation and forest degradation through integrated conservation and sustainable land management practices, guided by the development and implementation of the Territorial and Environmental Management Plan (PGTA). PGTA serves as a strategic framework for planning and executing activities, ensuring alignment with community priorities, cultural values, and governance structures. Core project activities include forest protection, ethnozoning, participatory land-use planning, and capacity-building programs designed to strengthen local governance and enhance resilience.
The project is implemented through a partnership among the Rio Branco community associations: DOA TXATO, WAYPA, and the WITI Indigenous Association, with technical support from Centro de Estudos Rioterra, a non-profit organization dedicated to promoting sustainable development models in the Amazon region. Additionally, a financial mechanism—AICA REDD—was established to ensure transparency and accountability, managing resource distribution according to terms authorized by the Associations.
The project area is located within the Rio Branco Indigenous Territory (IT), encompassing 3 municipalities in the state of Rondonia, Brazil. The territory spans 235,773 hectares within the Amazon biome and is home to the Arikapu, Aruu, Djeoromitxi, Sakirabiar, Diahoi, Kampe, Kanoe, Makurap, and Tupari peoples. Their profound cultural and spiritual connection to the forest informs the projects priorities.
Prior to implementation, the territory faced threats from illegal logging, land encroachment, and limited institutional capacity, which endangered both the forest ecosystem and the cultural integrity of the Rio Branco communities.
Through targeted interventions, the project is expected to achieve an average annual reduction of approx 60,988 tCO₂e, totalling around 2,439,529 tCO₂e over the 40y crediting period.
vcs-584: The project activity involved implementing rice husk based cogeneration facility of 2.5 MW condensing cum extraction turbine and one 22 TPH boiler. The steam and electricity generated from the project activity replaces the coal fired boiler of 12 TPH and electricity generated by the fossil fuel intensive state grid system.
vcs-5841: The EnviroServ Waste-to-Energy (WtE) Grouped Project will involve the diversion of municipal solid waste (MSW) from landfill sites in the Republic of South Africa for thermal treatment through controlled mass-burn incineration. The heat generated from combustion will be used to produce steam for electricity generation, with the exported electricity displacing fossil fuel–based grid power.
vcs-5842:
The project “UNITÁN II: AFFORESTATION AND REFORESTATION GROUPED PROJECT WITH VARIETY OF NATIVE SPECIES IN THE ARGENTINE CHACO” is an afforestation grouped project in northeastern Argentina that establishes and restores woody cover through planting and human-assisted natural regeneration of native (Quebracho Colorado and other native species). and complementary species (Eucalyptus), A core strength of UNITÁN’s approach is reforesting with native species to supply future wood needs and thereby reduce extraction pressure on remaining native forests, central to the company’s mission of restoration and environmental recovery on lands degraded by prior agriculture.

The project implements integrated, privately managed plantations that avoid new extractions from native forests and brings soil protection, improved water runoff regulation, and biodiversity co-benefits while generating practical knowledge on native-species silviculture.

As a grouped project, its eligible areas are distributed across the Argentine Chaco. Within this region, current grazing and cropland areas generally derive from previous deforestation and present varying degrees of degradation associated with extensive, low-input land use. The grouped design enables phased inclusion of new Project Activity Instances (PAIs) as sites are validated and planted under the same methodological and safeguard framework.

The first PAI is located on the Los Brotes farm (department of El Colorado, Formosa Province) and will establish afforestation on 285 ha, delivering an estimated ≈66.298 tCO₂e of net GHG removals over the project’s 43-year duration (i.e., an average of ≈1.542 tCO₂e per year). Further PAIs will be incorporated as sites meet the eligibility criteria and are implemented under the project’s management and monitoring system.

vcs-5845: The NMPP aims to protect and restore the vast peatland, mangrove, and swamp forests from the threat of conversion into timber logging for large-scale pulp and paper production, palm oil plantation, and aquaculture, as the main deforestation drivers in North Kalimantan. It is a grouped project with a total area of 15,591 hectares. The project also aims to strengthen local communities, over 24,427 individuals that reside within 4 communities in the project zone, through inclusive participation, improved public services, and the development of sustainable livelihoods, ensuring economic resilience and social well-being. At the same time, it will safeguard biodiversity by conserving HCV areas, restoring degraded habitats, and protecting threatened species; the vast area of NMPP is home to over 28 RTE species. This project is pursuing certification under the following Verra methodologies: VM0007 for Emission Reductions from Deforestation and Forest Degradation, VM0047 for Afforestation, Reforestation, and Revegetation, and VM0033 for Tidal Wetland Restoration. vcs-5846:
Beetle Regen: Advancing Low-Emission Agriculture through Improved Land Management in Aurangabad, Maharashtra adopts the VCS Methodology VM0042 – Methodology for Improved Agricultural Land Management (Version 2.2)1 to implement sustainable cotton cultivation practices aimed at increasing soil organic carbon (SOC) stocks and reducing greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions in Aurangabad, Maharashtra, India.
The project transitions farmers from conventional to a suite of improved land management practices. These include conservation tillage, intercropping with red gram and green gram (90-day cycle), crop residue retention, application of biofertilizers, reduced nitrogen fertilizer use (~75 kg/ha average), and organic amendments such as farmyard manure (>3 t/ha), neem oil (~1 L/ha), and Dashaparni Ark (10–25 kg/ha). These measures enhance soil health, improve nitrogen use efficiency, and significantly increase carbon sequestration in the soil
vcs-5848:
The Lunga Luswishi Carbon Enhancement Project aims to secure the long-term financial viability of the Lunga Luswishi landscape and protect this critical wilderness area and the biodiversity it contains whilst generating financial, climate and social impact return through the sale of carbon credits. This is achieved by developing a large-scale woody savannah fire management project on the eligible miombo forested land in the landscape focused on reducing the methane (CH4) and nitrous oxide (N2O) emissions as result of the shift in the fire seasonality from Late Dry Season (LDS, August, September and October) to Early Dry Season (EDS, May, June and July), managed via a tailored prescribed burning program. Indeed, EDS fires, which are lower in intensity than LDS fires due to reduced fuel loads, produce fewer greenhouse gas emissions and spread more slowly across the landscape with a higher degree of patchiness compared to LDS. Ultimately, the shifted fire regime will directly contribute to reducing forest degradation and enhancing the forest carbon stock in the Lunga Luswishi landscape, in addition to directly reducing GHG emissions. 
The project will also help increase the economic wellbeing of the communities bordering the project area and support poverty alleviation in an area that otherwise offers few alternative economic livelihoods beyond subsistence farming.

Rainforest Builder Ltd is an integrated tropical forest restoration company founded in 2022 to pioneer tropical forest ecosystem restoration as a commercial undertaking, by combining the best restoration science with professional forestry industry practice to deliver ecosystem restoration at unprecedented quality and scale. Rainforest Builder’s projects aim to return degraded formerly forested lands to primary levels of biomass, biodiversity and structural complexity rapidly and resiliently, in partnership with a range of stakeholders. 
The ARR VCS-CCB grouped project aims to restore approximately 100,000 ha of degraded land by 2040 within Protected Areas in the Guinée Forestière Region of southeastern Guinea. The project will deliver sustainable ecosystem restoration through diversified native mixed-species plantings that re-establish the structure and function of natural rainforests, enhancing ecological connectivity and mitigating the degradation effects resulting from existing land uses such as small-scale agriculture, grazing, and timber extraction. 
Central to this endeavour is the implementation of best-practice silviculture and planting methods, using mixes of framework tree species that are carefully selected to provide key structural and functional roles. 
The Climate, Community, and Biodiversity goals of the project are to re-establish and protect natural forest landscapes, recovering threatened biodiversity in a globally important conservation hotspot, sequestering CO2 and improving the provision of ecosystem services including water regulation, nutrient cycling, and climate regulation. 
Long-term sustainability is enhanced through the creation of small-scale commercial harvesting areas to provide local communities with secure job opportunities and diversified long-term revenue streams. Monitoring of forest and vegetation composition, biodiversity and community impacts will be conducted over the long term to assess the progress of the initiatives.

The Increasing Carbon Stocks through the Reforestation of the Communal Forests of Ndélélé and Bétaré-Oya Project (commercial name: Iroko Restoration Project – Cameroon) is a 40-year grouped ARR AFOLU project aiming to restore degraded communal forests, increase long-term carbon stocks, and support sustainable livelihoods in Cameroon’s East Region. The initial project instance covers 8,289 ha within the Ndélélé and Bétaré-Oya Communal Forests and combines native forest restoration with cocoa-based agroforestry.
Native forest restoration is implemented through direct planting of over 25 native tree species, while cocoa agroforestry integrates cocoa with shade trees to balance durable carbon sequestration and community income generation. The project is located in the Congo Basin, where forests have been degraded by unsustainable logging, slash-and-burn agriculture, charcoal production, and artisanal mining, and where natural regeneration remains limited.
Restoration activities generate net GHG removals through increased above- and below-ground biomass. Over the 40-year crediting period, total cumulative removals are estimated at approximately 3.3 million tCO₂e.
The project’s climate objective is to increase long-term forest carbon stocks while generating high-quality, durable carbon credits. Community objectives include sustained local employment, transparent benefit-sharing mechanisms developed through an ongoing FPIC process, establishment of cocoa agroforestry systems, allocation of a share of carbon revenues to communal development funds, increased participation and economic benefits for women, and strengthened local governance and land-use planning. Biodiversity objectives include restoring native forest structure and function using locally adapted species, integrating restored areas into conservation and protected zones within Communal Forest Management Plans, and maintaining high-shade cocoa systems that enhance habitat connectivity and increase forest cover.
vcs-5859:
The AgriCapture Latin America Rice Methane Project will generate emission reductions under VCS Methodology VM0051: Improved Management in Rice Production Systems. The project supports rice growers in Latin America in adopting improved irrigation practices to reduce both greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and water use. 
Within the project, growers will implement improved irrigation practices. Prior to project implementation, rice growers in the project practiced continuous flood irrigation. Continuous flooding creates an anaerobic soil environment that fosters methane producing microbes (Searchinger & Waite, 2014). Methane emissions rise as the duration of the flooded period increases, due to the buildup of these microbes (Searchinger & Waite, 2014). By introducing periods of drying that allow oxygen to reenter the soil, improved irrigation practices, like single-drainage and alternate wetting and drying (AWD), can significantly reduce methane emissions. Research indicates that AWD lowers methane emissions by 47% while also decreasing water consumption by up to 39% (Gao, 2024; Atwill R. L., 2020). 
Participating growers may also transition from transplanted rice to direct seeded rice, another improved irrigation practice. Traditional transplanted rice involves rice seedlings being grown in a nursery before being planted in puddled fields (Ishfaq, Akbar, Anjum, & Anwar-Ijl-Haq, 2020). The process requires a prohibitive amount of labor, and puddling the field requires large amounts of irrigation (Ishfaq, Akbar, Anjum, & Anwar-Ijl-Haq, 2020). Additionally, the puddled fields established before planting increases methane emissions due to increasing the period of anaerobic conditions (Reddy, et al., 2025). When compared to transplanted rice, direct seeded rice reduces methane emissions and water consumption by 70% and 8-12% respectively (Reddy, et al., 2025; Ishfaq, Akbar, Anjum, & Anwar-Ijl-Haq, 2020).

The project utilizes Thermal Energy Hub Technology to generate high-temperature flue gas, which is then directed through a steam boiler to recover heat and produce steam. All generated steam is supplied for heating purposes to the coal mine. 
The project utilizes Thermal Energy Hub Technology to generate high-temperature flue gas, which is then directed through a steam boiler to recover heat and produce steam. All generated steam is supplied for heating purposes to the coal mine. vcs-5861: The project proposed to be carried out by Motion Energy Group (ME) in accordance with VCS methodology VM0038, Methodology for Electric Vehicle Charging Systems v1.0. This grouped project avoids greenhouse gas emissions through the displacement of internal combustion engine (ICE) with electric vehicles (EVs) and plug in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs) through support for the provision of EVs and EV charging infrastructure. The project will incorporate EV fleets, providing charging data through onboard telematics, and EV charging networks, providing charging data through smart charger data collection and other means described in VM0038. This project is anticipated to include both LDVs and HDVs (e-buses and e-trucks), and a range of EV charging networks including both L2 and DC Fast Chargers.
vcs-5862: The One Acre Fund (OAF) Rwanda Forest Landscape Restoration Project (FLR) promotes multifunctional tree planting in agricultural lands through the provision of customized tree packages to smallholder farmers in Rwanda. These tree packages assist in addressing soil erosion concerns, soil fertility, farm boundary demarcation, and biomass needs. The project is a joint VCS and Sustainable Development Verified Impact Standard (SDVista) grouped Afforestation, Reforestation, and Revegetation project in Rwanda. Currently, this project is implemented in seven districts including Bugesera, Rwamagana, Kamonyi, Muhanga, Karongi, Nyamasheke and Rusizi with expansion plans in all areas of Rwanda.  One Acre Fund curates its agroforestry tree packages to include a mix of Indigenous and non-native species that provide farmers with a sustainable source of fuelwood and fodder as well as co-benefits including soil fertility, erosion control, and windbreaks, among others. Farmers are instructed on how planting some trees in the package on the boundary and contour of croplands will assist in erosion control and provide fuel or fodder provisions, while planting others within crop fields will lead to improved soil fertility and hydrologic function. One Acre Fund also offers high-value trees, such as fruit and nut trees, along with the agroforestry tree packages as further incentive, food source, and income for farmers.  The program is estimated to generate a total of 3.2 million tonnes of carbon removals over 30 years and an average of 105,000 tonnes per year.
vcs-5863:
The One Acre Fund Limited (OAF) Munda Otsogola Program (MOP) is a grouped Afforestation, Reforestation, and Revegetation (ARR) project implemented under the Verified Carbon Standard (VCS) and Sustainable Development Verified Impact Standard (SD VISta) in central and southern Malawi. The project promotes multifunctional tree planting on agricultural lands, fallow areas, and around homesteads by providing smallholder farmers with subsidized packages of agroforestry and specialty trees, including fruit and nut species.
Prior to project implementation, participating areas reflect typical smallholder farming systems in Malawi, characterized by fragmented plots dominated by annual staple crops such as maize and legumes. These landscapes face declining soil fertility, soil erosion, and limited on-farm tree cover, driven by long-term Miombo woodland degradation, agricultural expansion, fuelwood harvesting, and charcoal production. Malawi has experienced among the highest historical deforestation rates in the Southern African Development Community (SADC), increasing pressure on soil and water resources and vulnerability to climate change.
The project promotes climate-smart agriculture practices, particularly agroforestry, to address these challenges. Evidence from Malawi and the SADC region shows that agroforestry can improve soil health, enhance crop productivity, reduce erosion, and strengthen resilience to climate variability, including erratic rainfall and extreme weather events. Agroforestry systems also contribute to climate change mitigation through increased biomass and soil carbon sequestration.
OAF curates tree packages that include native and non-native species to meet farmer needs for fuelwood, fodder, food, and income, while delivering environmental co-benefits such as soil fertility enhancement, erosion control, and windbreaks. vcs-587: The project is designed to protect 7 666 hectares of native Tasmanian forest which would, if not for the project, continue to undergo selective logging or be clear-felled and converted to pasture.
vcs-5871:
The project activity entails installation of a biogas plant in the city of Lahore, Pakistan. The raw feed to the biogas plant shall be cattle manure. The biogas generated shall be utilized in the industry for thermal energy generation. The project activity is implemented by Punjab Power Development Company (PPDCL). 

In the absence of project activity, cattle manure generated from approximately 24,000 animals was dumped openly in large grounds and vacant spaces. With no formal collection or treatment system in place, the waste would mix with sewerage water and rainwater to form slurry pools. This uncontrolled degradation of organic matter created unhygienic conditions for the local community and led to the uncontrolled release of methane, directly into the atmosphere. The absence of proper waste management practices not only contributed to significant methane emissions but also posed serious public health and environmental hazards. Biogas generated in the project is a direct replacement of baseline CNG use in the industry. Management of cattle dung for the production of biogas is helping in reducing the environmental pollution and improving the hygiene condition for the inhabitants in the vicinity. 

The biogas is being produced using Continuous Stirred-Tank Reactor (CSTR) technology and is upgraded to fuel-grade quality. Technical details of the equipment installed in the project are provided in section 1.11 of this PD. The project is expected to commission by Jan 2026.
vcs-5872: The proposed ARR project “Project Aranyam: Building Climate Resilient Communities in Maharashtra and Gujarat Through Agroforestry Practices” is a grouped project activity that aims to restore approximately 10,000 hectares of degraded land in the Indian states of Maharashtra and Gujarat. This grouped project activity is being developed by Clean Max Aranyam Private Limited. This project will include plantation through a mix of native and agroforestry species. By planting diverse tree species, the project will act as a carbon sink and thus, support towards climate change mitigation. Beyond climate benefits, the project delivers strong social and other co-benefits towards jobs creation and livelihood improvements for men and women in the local regions and also have positive impacts on biodiversity for long term basis.
vcs-5873: The Gunung Lumut Landscape Project (GLLP) in Paser Regency, East Kalimantan Province, Indonesia, spans approximately 116,001 hectares of predominantly lowland forest. The project is designed to protect biodiversity, watersheds, and indigenous heritage. GLLP integrates production forest (Unit I) and protected forest (Unit II), including the sacred Gunung Lumut Protected Forest. The project shifts traditional timber concessions toward ecosystem services such as carbon sequestration, aiming to restore ecological functions, prevent habitat fragmentation, and empower communities. Surveys have identified critically endangered hornbills, 118 bird species, 20 mammals, and rare flora, confirming the area’s exceptional biodiversity. The GLLP project area also faces persistent challenges including decades of illegal logging and forest conversion into palm and rubber plantations, with Unit II heavily logged between 2000–2005 despite its protected status. These pressures stem from limited awareness and livelihood opportunities, driving communities toward unsustainable practices. In response to these challenges, GLLP advances patrols, reforestation, community engagement, and sustainable resource management, embracing the principle of “strong sustainability” that treats natural capital as an irreplaceable foundation. The project is expected to generate 941,061 tCO2e annually, totaling 47 million tCO2e over 50 years.
vcs-5874:
This project is designed to achieve Gold Level outcomes for climate change mitigation and adaptation, community development, and biodiversity conservation. Over its 40-year lifetime, the project is expected to remove approximately 3,918,539 tCO₂e through the restoration and long-term protection of 4,527 hectares of native mangroves, implemented in partnership with local governments and communities. By strengthening coastal ecosystems and enhancing ecosystem services, the project increases resilience to climate-related risks such as cyclones, flooding, sea-level rise, and extreme heat, while improving the adaptive capacity of both communities and biodiversity.
 
The Project Zone is home to approximately 30,000 people across 60 coastal villages, many of whom are smallholder and marginalized communities facing high levels of poverty, limited access to basic services, and significant exposure to climate and disaster risks. Project activities deliver both immediate and long-term benefits by improving livelihoods, financial security, and social inclusion, with a strong focus on women and vulnerable groups, thereby reducing climate vulnerability and enhancing overall well-being.
 
Located in the coastal regions of Trincomalee, Batticaloa, and Ampara, the project area qualifies as a Key Biodiversity Area within a critically endangered arid-zone mangrove ecosystem. The region supports globally threatened and vulnerable species and plays a vital role in maintaining ecological integrity. By restoring degraded mangrove habitats, preventing further deforestation, addressing climate-related threats, raising stakeholder awareness, building local capacity, and mobilizing technical and financial resources, the project delivers lasting benefits for biodiversity conservation while supporting sustainable coastal development.
vcs-5876:
The ARR agroforestry Program aims to address the pressing challenges of land degradation, and food insecurity by promoting sustainable agroforestry practices. The program will focus on transforming agricultural landscapes through the implementation of agroforestry systems, enhancing both the productivity and environmental sustainability of farming conditions of smallholder farmers.
The Program will be implemented in partnership with Asosiasaun Movimento Kablaki Timor-Leste (AMK- TL) which is an independent non-governmental organization. AMK -TL has been engaging farmers in planting trees and adopting agroforestry since 2022 and so far, the project has restored 1,255 hectares of land in seven municipalities (Aileu, Ainaro, Covalima, Dili, Ermera, Manatuto and Manufahi) by adding shade (mahogany) to existing coffee plantations. 
The proposed program activities for the project include the establishment of an additional 10,000 hectares of agroforestry in the municipalities of Manufahi, Atauro, Ainaro, Covalima, Bobonaro, Ambeno, Manatuto, Alieu Ermera and Liquica. The planting will be done in three phases, with each phase, planting 3,333 trees per year. The proposed agroforestry system incorporates boundary and alley cropping with cash crops/fruit trees (such as oranges) and food crops (annual crops). This approach offers multiple benefits, including providing shade, preventing soil erosion and enhancing soil fertility through nitrogen fixation, and supplying sustainable sources of food and fruits. 
Other program activities that will be implemented to promote community wellbeing include local commercialization of cash crops harvested from the agroforestry system, to diversify household income. Capacity building for smallholder farmers and their families will be widely conducted to equip them with skills, knowledge and tools to successfully grow and maintain their agroforestry systems and actively participate in organized farmer groups.
vcs-5877:
The Agroforestry Program to be implemented in Karene, Sierra Leone aims to restore degraded lands, enhance biodiversity, and improve local livelihoods, all while ensuring equity and respect for customary land rights. It aligns with national land reform efforts and international standards for sustainable development and carbon market practices.
The key stakeholders for the Program include local communities (smallholder farmers), traditional authorities, and supporting government agencies. The eligible area encompasses approximately 15,412 hectares across nine community-owned lands within the Sanda Loko chiefdom. Land in this region is held under customary tenure by community members and families, with rights typically inherited. Traditional authorities, such as chiefs, act as custodians, managing land allocation and resolving disputes. 
The Program activities are centered on the establishment of a diversified agroforestry system with small holder farmers to increase tree cover in non-forest areas.  This diversified agroforestry system will include cash crops, food crops, wood trees and others with to provide economic and food security benefits to farmers and their families. The Program will engage 1,050 of farmers who are organized in 13 associations, who will be responsible of planting and maintaining the trees. 
The initiative integrates agroforestry interventions with a strong social inclusion framework. Recognizing the central role of women and youth in local resilience, the Program is committed to their participation at all levels. Activities are designed to build their skills in sustainable farming and entrepreneurship, ensure their accessibility to training and decision-making processes, and foster economic empowerment through support for small businesses and savings groups. This project implements an integrated Municipal Solid Waste (MSW) treatment system to reduce landfill disposal and recover material and energy from mixed municipal waste streams. The system combines hyperbaric hydrothermal processing, automated post-sorting, and anaerobic digestion in a non-incineration process.

Incoming unsorted MSW is treated using hyperbaric hydrothermal technology, where saturated steam under elevated temperature and pressure is applied in a sealed rotating vessel. This process de-polymerizes complex ligno-cellulosic structures, sterilizes the waste, increases biodegradability, and reduces overall waste volume without producing dioxins or hazardous air pollutants. No upstream manual pre-sorting is required.

Following treatment, the processed material undergoes automated mechanical separation to recover recyclable fractions such as plastics, metals, and glass for downstream recycling. The organic fraction is directed to anaerobic digestion, where biodegradable material is converted into biogas and stabilized digestate under controlled conditions. Captured biogas is utilized on-site to meet energy needs, including thermal requirements of the process, reducing reliance on external fossil fuels. The remaining digestate is processed into compost or soil-enhancement products, subject to regulatory requirements.

By diverting MSW from landfill disposal and stabilizing organic waste, the project avoids methane emissions that would otherwise occur under baseline landfill conditions while supporting resource recovery and sustainable waste management. The modular system design allows scalability to accommodate varying waste volumes while maintaining consistent environmental performance. Overall, the project contributes to greenhouse gas emission reductions, resource recovery, and sustainable waste management aligned with circular economy principles.

The REDD+ Cabeceira do Xingu Project is a deforestation prevention initiative implemented across 21 private rural properties in the municipalities of Feliz Natal and Vera, in the state of Mato Grosso, Brazil. Located within the Legal Amazon, the project operates exclusively on private lands, with areas distributed within municipal boundaries and duly mapped. Its central objective is to prevent the unplanned conversion of native Amazon forests, composed of mosaics of open and dense tropical forests. To achieve this, the project adopts binding land management agreements and land-use planning measures. 
Project actions include on-the-ground patrols combined with satellite-based monitoring. Rapid response mechanisms to deforestation alerts and forest fire prevention are also in place. The project supports the environmental regularization of properties, including Legal Reserves and Permanent Preservation Areas (APPs). A conservative Monitoring, Reporting, and Verification (MRV) system is applied, aligned with VCS/REDD+ requirements, including leakage management and permanence risk mitigation. Emission reductions are calculated based on a conservative baseline derived from spatial modeling of deforestation risk and carbon stocks. The region is characterized by rising land values, irregular enforcement, and recurrent wildfires. Historically, there have been few economic incentives for forest conservation. In this context, carbon credits emerge as a mechanism to enhance the value of standing forests. Four small and medium-sized producers are direct beneficiaries during the initial phase

The AgriCapture South Asia Rice Methane Project will generate emission reductions under VCS Methodology VM0051: Improved Management in Rice Production Systems. The project supports rice growers in South Asia in adopting improved irrigation practices to reduce both greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and water use. 
Within the project, growers will implement improved irrigation practices. Prior to project implementation, rice growers in the project practiced continuous flood irrigation. Continuous flooding creates an anaerobic soil environment that fosters methane producing microbes (Searchinger & Waite, 2014). Methane emissions rise as the duration of the flooded period increases, due to the buildup of these microbes (Searchinger & Waite, 2014). By introducing periods of drying that allow oxygen to reenter the soil, improved irrigation practices, like single-drainage and alternate wetting and drying (AWD), can significantly reduce methane emissions. Research indicates that AWD lowers methane emissions by 47% while also decreasing water consumption by up to 39% (Gao, 2024; Atwill R. L., 2020). 
Participating growers may also transition from transplanted rice to direct seeded rice, another improved irrigation practice. Traditional transplanted rice involves rice seedlings being grown in a nursery before being planted in puddled fields (Ishfaq, Akbar, Anjum, & Anwar-Ijl-Haq, 2020). The process requires a prohibitive amount of labor, and puddling the field requires large amounts of irrigation (Ishfaq, Akbar, Anjum, & Anwar-Ijl-Haq, 2020). Additionally, the puddled fields established before planting increases methane emissions due to increasing the period of anaerobic conditions (Reddy, et al., 2025). When compared to transplanted rice, direct seeded rice reduces methane emissions and water consumption by 70% and 8-12% respectively (Reddy, et al., 2025; Ishfaq, Akbar, Anjum, & Anwar-Ijl-Haq, 2020).
vcs-5891:
The Forest Landscape Restoration in North Sulawesi Province project in Indonesia, in the eastern seaboard of North Sulawesi, aims to enrich and restore 6,000 hectares of degraded and deforested land, with the potential to expand to 10,000 hectares. The project will work with smallholder and local community farmers to implement a diverse mix of agroforestry and reforestation models tailored to local conditions and needs.
The project is located within the tropical rainforest ecosystem in Indonesia's North Sulawesi Province. The region has experienced severe degradation from monocultures and slash-and-burn practices, leading to soil infertility, reduced forest cover, and fire-prone grasses that stall natural regrowth and segment wildlife habitats.
Through agroforestry-based plantations and targeted reforestation efforts, the project will support smallholders in reviving farmland and restoring forests, ultimately improving livelihoods and protecting biodiversity. Farmers receive training in regenerative methods (e.g., intercropping native timber and fruit species), access to high-value saplings, and implementing soil revitalisation techniques. By placing community leadership at the centre of these initiatives, the project enhances climate resilience, prevents additional deforestation, and fosters a sustainable future for local ecosystems.
Stakeholder engagement is central to the project’s success. It will involve Thryve.Earth, the Masarang Foundation, landowners, government entities, community leaders, traditional authorities, local communities (including youth, women, and marginalized groups), research institutions, and financiers.
Over a project-crediting period of 40 years, the project's key outcomes are to sequester over 6.35 million tCO2e (approximately an annual average of 158,764 tCO2e emission reductions), improve biodiversity, and enhance the livelihoods of participating households and local communities.
vcs-5893:
This project, located in Bangalore, Karnataka, India, implements an innovative waste management solution using Black Soldier Fly (BSF) larvae-based aerobic composting technology. The facility processes 300 metric tons per day (TPD) of organic municipal solid waste (wet fraction only), diverting it from landfills to a controlled biological treatment system.
BSF larvae (Hermetia illucens) accelerate the decomposition of organic matter under optimized aerobic conditions, producing nutrient-rich compost for agricultural use and larvae biomass for animal feed—supporting circular economy principles. The system ensures efficient stabilization of organic matter while preventing anaerobic conditions, thereby minimizing methane emissions.
By replacing conventional landfill disposal, the project avoids methane (CH₄) emissions—a greenhouse gas with a Global Warming Potential (GWP) 28 times that of CO₂. Emission reductions are quantified using the CDM methodology ACM0022: Alternative Waste Treatment Processes (Version 03.0) under the VCS Standard.
Prior to implementation, organic MSW was disposed of in unmanaged landfills without methane capture, resulting in significant GHG emissions. The project introduces a sustainable alternative aligned with climate mitigation and resource recovery goals.
The proposed activity is expected to generate an average annual GHG emission reduction of approximately 58,940 tCO₂e, with a total of about 589,401 tCO₂e over a 10-year fixed crediting period.
The project is designed as a grouped project, and this is the first project activity instance (PAI#01) under the group. Additional project activities will be added in the future after validation, enabling scalability and broader impact.
Mukka Protein Limited serves as the project proponent and developer, responsible for implementation, management, and monitoring.

Project Sierra Verde is a grouped Afforestation, Reforestation, and Revegetation (ARR) project eligible under the Verified Carbon Standard. The project delivers climate mitigation, community livelihood, and biodiversity benefits by restoring degraded grasslands and croplands through native forest restoration and agroforestry systems. Sierra Verde operates in Quirino and Nueva Vizcaya provinces, Philippines, covering a grouped boundary of over 720,000 hectares. The first project instance is in Quirino Province, covering approximately 5,057 hectares with potential expansion to about 7,500 hectares, the majority of which is managed under lands owned by local Indigenous Peoples. 

Project activities include establishing nurseries for native and indigenous tree species, direct planting of native forest species, and integrating coffee under native shade trees in multi-layered agroforestry systems. Local communities participate in seedling production, planting, maintenance, and protection, linking forest restoration with sustainable livelihoods.

These interventions promote biomass accumulation in newly established reforestation systems. Over a 40-year crediting period, the first project instance is expected to remove approximately 2.59 million tonnes of CO₂e, equivalent to an average annual removal of about 64,788 tonnes of CO₂e.

Telangana has over 5.8 million marginal farmers (Agricultural Census, 2021), most cultivating less than 2 hectares and increasingly exposed to climate risks such as groundwater depletion, soil degradation, and declining yields. These vulnerabilities were amplified by extreme events like the 2020 floods, which affected over 0.4 million hectares and caused losses of about ₹2,000 crore (Telangana State Disaster Management Report, 2021). With climate variability intensifying, urgent and scalable solutions are needed to strengthen farmer resilience.

Harit Bharat – Telangana is a grouped Afforestation, Reforestation, and Revegetation (ARR) project promoting agroforestry on private and community lands to generate carbon income while restoring ecosystems. The project aims to cover 212,070 hectares through diversified systems combining native species, fruit trees, timber species, and non-timber forest products. These interventions enhance carbon sequestration, soil health, biodiversity, and on-farm resources such as shade and fodder.

The first plantation instance covers over 136,000 hectares of private land and 53,000 hectares of community and Gram Panchayat land, with remaining areas to be planted in future instances. The project is expected to benefit more than 134,000 marginal farmers and generate around 15,000 person-days of employment annually.

Aligned with India’s Nationally Determined Contributions, the project contributes to the national target of creating an additional carbon sink of 56,787,786 tCO₂e by 2052, while demonstrating a replicable, nature-based solution for climate mitigation, adaptation, and sustainable livelihoods in Telangana.

Project Uramia is a large-scale, community-led REDD+ initiative in Colombia’s Chocó Basin, one of the world’s most biodiverse forest regions. Located in the Bajo Atrato region (Río Sucio and Carmen del Darién, Chocó Department), the project protects 255,220 hectares of intact tropical forest across six Indigenous resguardos. Project Uramia applies a rights-based, community-centered conservation model combining active forest protection, community-based monitoring and patrols, and strengthened Indigenous governance through elected Project Councils and participatory land-use planning. The project promotes sustainable livelihoods—including non-timber forest product value chains, agroforestry, and artisanal activities—with a strong focus on women and youth, reducing reliance on destructive land-use practices.

The project targets Avoided Unplanned Deforestation (AUD) under Verra VCS Methodology VM0048 v1.0, with a 40-year crediting period (May 2024–May 2064). It is expected to generate approximately 1.0 million tCO₂e annually, totaling over 40 million tCO₂e over the crediting period.

The Family Forest Carbon Program – Fields & Forests (F&F) project, administered by the Family Forest Impact Foundation, works with family and other non-industrial private landowners in the US South and Southeast to transition underused row crop and pastureland into forests, creating sustainable income opportunities and growing trees to mitigate climate change. The program assists landowners with ongoing revenue and the cost of planting new, native forests where forests have not existed for at least 10 years, resulting in healthy, productive, carbon-sequestering forests, reliable income, a long-term asset for
landowners, and other environmental benefits.

FFCP uses a grouped project design to group small landowners together, including small ownerships that have been under-represented in the voluntary carbon market. Additionally, F&F engages with heirs’ property landowners and supports the development of clear title, unblocking a barrier for those landowners. For all participating landowners, F&F helps navigate the voluntary carbon market and ensures income, building timber assets, and benefit sharing.

FFCP provides payments, operational and technical assistance, and ongoing stewardship to ensure the reforestation of acres enrolled. The first F&F cohorts plant loblolly pine, a commercial species, within its native range in the US Southeast. The practice requires replanting after an optional harvest rotation estimated to occur 25 – 30 years after project start for each cohort and utilizes a Permanence Fund to ensure replanting and continued technical and stewardship assistance for alumni properties for continuation of the practice activity through 100 years.
vcs-5919:
The Family Forest Carbon Program – North (FFCP-NORTH), administered by the Family Forest Impact Foundation (FFIF), is an innovative, incentive-based program engaging private family and other non-industrial private forest landowners throughout the United States in improved forest management practices, furthering forest health, carbon sequestration and storage, and other environmental conservation and protection practices. 

Through its grouped project design, the FFCP engages and achieves economies of scale with small, non-industrial forest landowners, reaching ownerships that have been largely unrepresented in voluntary carbon markets. The FFCP-NORTH solves challenges to small forest holdings participation in carbon projects by reducing cost and complexity of participation. 

FFCP-NORTH provides incentive payments, technical assistance, and ongoing stewardship support to forest landowners to implement climate-smart practices that increase sequestration and storage of carbon, helping family landowners transition to long-term, sustainable forest management.

Lamantin mangrove restoration and conservation project, developed by Blue Coast Carbon, is a community-based large-scale mangrove conservation project in Guinea, West Africa.
The project will be located in an area along the northern coasts of Guinea, covering a total of 73,751 hectares of mangrove forests. The overall project objective is to generate high-quality carbon credits based on greenhouse gases (GHGs) emission reduction and avoidance, that will sustainably finance the project and result in economic benefits for the local communities. GHGs emission reductions are expected to be generated by avoiding unplanned deforestation by providing alternative income to local communities through the implementation of a series of activities, including those supporting the use of efficient cookstoves, solar salt production systems, education campaigns, and supporting the development of apiculture, aquaculture and ecotourism.
Carbon dioxide (CO2) removals will be generated by restoring areas of degraded mangrove forests with the involvement of local communities, supporting local livelihoods and alleviating poverty. An ecosystem-based approach will be used for habitat restoration, aiming at improving hydrology and environmental conditions, with minimal need for re-planting.
The project will restore a total of 2,725 hectares of degraded mangrove forests and protect a total of 73,751 hectares from deforestation, contributing to the protection of coastal communities from climate change, the conservation of the world’s biodiversity and to mitigating climate change. The project’s climate benefits over the crediting period include the sequestration and avoided emission of 3,374,658 tCO2e.
vcs-5923:
Balbuzard mangrove restoration and conservation project is a community-based mangrove conservation project. The project will be located in an area along the central coasts of Guinea (West Africa), covering a total of 97,305 hectares of mangrove forests.
Mangroves are amongst the planet’s most productive and complex ecosystems, and are recognized for their superior carbon sequestration capabilities compared to terrestrial forests. Throughout West Africa, the livelihoods of coastal populations depend heavily on access to natural resources. Mangroves are integral to many of those resources, providing wood and non-wood forest products, coastal protection, conservation of biological diversity, provision of habitat, spawning grounds and nutrients for a variety of fish and shellfish, and salt production. Many communities rely on mangrove wood as a primary fuel source for curing fish and other purposes, and urban expansion and intensifying demands for charcoal, fuel wood, and land for agriculture are growing drivers of mangrove deforestation and degradation.
The overall project objective is to generate high-quality carbon credits based on greenhouse gases emission reduction and avoidance, that will sustainably finance the project and result in economic benefits for the local communities. GHGs emission reductions will be generated by avoiding unplanned deforestation by providing alternative income to local communities through the implementation of activities supporting the use of efficient cookstoves, solar salt production systems, education campaigns, and supporting the development of apiculture, aquaculture and ecotourism.
CO2 removals will be generated by restoring areas of degraded mangrove forests with the involvement of local communities, alleviating poverty. The project will restore a total of 2,578 hectares of degraded mangrove forests and protect a total of 97,305 hectares from deforestation, contributing to the mitigation of climate change.
