Finally, the project will provide direct benefits to 17 or more pastoralist communities in form of funds for bursaries to support women and the poorest community members as well as to construct water capture structures and infrastructure for delivering livestock to market. The project is expected to remove more than 63 million tons CO2e over the project lifetime of 40 years, or nearly 1.6 million tons CO2e a year on average.
ccb-4724:
Xinjiang Altay Improved Grassland Management Project (hereafter as ‘the project’) is located in Altay City, Altay Prefecture, Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, China. The project aims to restore the local degraded grassland ecosystem by Improved sustainable grassland management measures, such as rotating grazing and grazing prohibition in the project area by building fences, and improving the degraded grassland ecosystem by reseeding high-quality local grass seeds. After the implementation of the project, the grassland will be scientifically and rationally utilized according to the health status of the local grassland ecosystem. Achieve long-term sustainable management of degraded local grasslands. The implementation of the project has significantly improved the local climate benefits, community benefits and biodiversity benefits. The project sponsor is Xinjiang Altay City Zhujin Investment Co., LTD..
The project is estimated to generate GHG emission removals of 18,687,019 tCO2-e in 40 years, with an average annual GHG emission removal of 467,175.475 tCO2-e.
ccb-4727:
The Trees for Farmers (TFF) Brazil ARR Grouped Project is an initiative located in the Brazilian Amazon biome. The project aims to establish, restore, and enhance vegetative cover through tree planting and assisted natural regeneration on degraded lands, bare soils, low-productivity areas, and areas undergoing regeneration, including Areas of Permanent Protection (APPs) and Legal Reserves (LRs) with limited natural regeneration.
Project activities focus on planting diverse mixes of native species to create biodiverse forests and woodlands, complemented where appropriate by non-invasive, ecosystem-compatible non-native species, and including endangered species.
Originally initiated by Rabobank Carbon Bank, the project is now led by The Green Branch as Project Proponent, in continued collaboration with Rabobank Brazil. Through its extensive farmer network, Rabobank Brazil supports expansion across a potential area exceeding 13 million hectares.
The first project instance covers 92.03 hectares planted within the Botuverá farm condominium (23,551.71 ha total) in Gaúcha do Norte, Mato Grosso. This instance is expected to generate average GHG removals of 756.32 tCO₂e per year.
Over its 40-year crediting period (2022–2062), the Grouped Project is expected to expand progressively, targeting 10,000 hectares of restored and planted land.
In addition to climate mitigation, the project seeks Climate, Community & Biodiversity (CCB) certification, achieving both Climate and Biodiversity Gold Levels. It also promotes local employment, capacity building, stakeholder engagement, and awareness of sustainable land use, biodiversity conservation, and climate change mitigation and adaptation.
ccb-4730:
Xinjiang Habahe Improved Grassland Management Project is located in Habahe County, Altay Region, Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, China. The Project aims to reduce the duration and amount of grazing on degraded grasslands by planting pasture grasses and improving grazing practices, in order to restore local degraded grassland systems and ensure grassland sustainability.
The project implemented sustainable grassland management on 91,976.85 hectares of degraded grassland through three measures: artificial grass planting, fencing and grazing ban, and rotational grazing. The implementation of the management measures can effectively increase the carbon stock and reduce non-CO2 greenhouse gas emissions, and ultimately achieve the purpose of greenhouse gas emission reduction. 
The project is expected to generate GHG emission removals of 6,283,832 tCO2e in 40 years, with an average annual GHG emission removals of 157,096 tCO2e.
ccb-4732: The NatureRe project is a grouped project that seeks to sustainably manage 4,500 ha, within which it is estimated there is potential to restore approximately 2,925 ha. This area corresponds to livestock-degraded lands in the Antioquia Department (Colombia), in three subregions: Magdalena Medio, Bajo Cauca, and Nordeste. The project aims to restore native forest species by applying different ANR models.
ccb-4744:
Paraguay, renowned for its abundant fauna and vegetation, has emerged as an area of concern regarding deforestation in Latin America. Both legal and illegal practices are slowly depleting these natural resources. Beyond their role as host of a vast biodiversity, the forests are also a crucial carbon sink.
The conversion of forests into cattle ranching, agriculture and timber production is one of the main drivers of legal deforestation in the country. Despite the Oriental Region of Paraguay has a zero-deforestation policy, the Occident, known as the Chaco Region, lost around 4.37 million hectares of forest between 2005 and 2020 to these practices (INFONA, 2022).
Under these circumstances, this project has been designed to preserve the Paraguayan Chaco forests by grouping landowners that have plans and permits to clear land but are willing to reduce this planned deforestation. Our goals include raising awareness about conservation and its positive effects, controlling logging practices and monitoring environmental and social indicators.
According to VCS Standard 4.5, eligible REDD activities are those that reduce net GHG emissions by reducing deforestation and/or forest degradation and, since the land is legally authorized to be converted to a non-forest area, project activities fall under the Avoiding Planned Deforestation category.
In the long term, specific actions related to biodiversity and community will be defined to be developed within the project framework.
Under the selected methodology, the carbon project is expected to generate a total of 45 million tCO2e in emission reductions over the course of a 30-year period. In other words, a yearly emission reduction equivalent to 1,5 million tCO2e.
ccb-4747:
The Pantanal biome is located in the center-west of Brazil, covering portions of the states of Mato Grosso and Mato Grosso do Sul. Considered the largest continuous freshwater wetland on the planet, this biome oscillates between terrestrial and aquatic phases, forming a mosaic of landscapes that provide great biodiversity of flora and fauna. Analyzing the historical context of the region where the Pantanal is located, there has been a considerable expansion of agricultural activities (the main local economic activity, mainly focused on the breeding of Pantanal cattle) and this factor, together with the high rates of forest fires in this area, results in a scenario of unsustainable exploitation of the natural resources of this biome.
Considering all the applicable legal requirements, landowners who have a surplus of native vegetation on their property and choose to preserve it, would fulfill the first requirement for obtaining economic incentives from the voluntary carbon market, through Reducing Emissions from Deforestation and Forest Degradation (REDD) through Avoided Planned Deforestation (APD). Given all this context, the implementation of the REDD+ Carbon Program on a scale for the Pantanal biome is possible, providing a model of sustainable economic development that can help to redress the balance, reconciling the conservation of environmental services with traditional economic activities. Biofílica Ambipar, in partnership with rural landowners in the Pantanal of Mato Grosso do Sul who are committed to promoting dialogue that benefits both the environment and sustainable economic development, aims to develop economic activities linked to the conservation of environmental services and all their ecological functions through the implementation of the Pantanal REDD+ Program.
ccb-4748:
The main objectives of this project are: First, to recover lands degraded by land uses related to deforestation, such as cattle ranching; through ecological restoration, agroforestry systems and assisted natural regeneration, to ensure the recovery of forests inhabited by many species of flora and fauna, including endangered species such as the brown spider monkey, the blue-billed curassow, capuchin monkey, the white-faced curassow, and the night monkey. Second, by implementing restoration corridors to reconnect wild populations within a grassland matrix to increase the flow of individuals, and therefore the genetic flow, of these populations and thus increase their resilience and probability of survival in the medium and long term. And third, to recover strategic areas that are degraded, such as the banks of rivers and other bodies of water or areas where grassland productivity is low. 
FPP Colombia (project proponent) is a non-profit organization promoting biodiversity research and conservation focusing on endangered primate species. FPP initiated one of Colombia's first studies and conservation programs for the brown spider monkey. FPP operates one of the longest-running research projects in Latin America, focusing on the brown spider monkey, one of the world's most endangered primates. FPP's activities have been concentrated in the Middle Magdalena River Valley, an area relatively little studied affected by human activity and part of a global biodiversity hotspot (Tumbes-Chocó-Magdalena).
The Proyecto de Vida Silvestre, an initiative of Ecopetrol SA, Fondo Acción and WCS, seeks to conserve biodiversity in 3 regions of Colombia of biological and cultural importance, but which face increasing pressures that threaten natural resources. Through the articulation of these conservation initiatives, sustainability is sought through the development of a grouped carbon project which will generate income from carbon credits to achieve the objectives of ecosystem recovery
ccb-4749:
The “Tajimat Pujut, Restoration and Conservation of the Alto Mayo Awajun Forests” is a grouped project jointly developed by the Federacion Regional Indigena Awajun del Alto Mayo (Regional Awajun Indigenous Federation of Alto Mayo - FERIAAM) and Conservation International Foundation (CI). FERIAAM is an indigenous territorial organization that groups and represents 16 indigenous Awajun communities (13 in the department of San Martin, and 3 in the department of Loreto). FERIAAM is the lead project proponent and CI is the co-proponent. The project is located in the provinces of Moyobamba, Rioja and Datem del Marañon, and covers an area of 235,455ha.
The main goal of the “Tajimat Pujut” project is to achieve the restoration and conservation of Awajun forests. In recent decades, deforestation within the Awajun communities has accelerated, with greater impact since 1990 after the opening of the Fernando Belaunde Terry highway. The increase in deforestation is mainly due to a heavy migration of people from the Andes and coastal region of Peru to the Amazon, causing a significant change in forest cover due to the expansion of the agricultural frontier and the illegal logging of high-value timber species. The forests of native communities have been replaced by commercial crops, mainly by farmers (tenants), invaders and illegal loggers. 
The project will focus on implementing strategies and activities to achieve better management of the Awajun territory, strengthen its governance and indigenous identity, restore degraded areas, and diversify sources of income and sustainable productive activities that secure wellbeing for the Awajun people. Tajimat Pujut expects to generate 8,788,206 tCO2eq over the 30 year project lifetime, with an average of 292,940 tCO2eq per year.
ccb-4756: The Bahenap Village Community has secured long-term management rights to a Village Forest area of around 10,700 hectares. The project will support the Village Forest Management Committee to sustainably manage this area for at least 25 years. The project proponent, Bentang Kalimantan Tangguh, will support the Bahenap Village Community to develop and implement sustainable forest management plans, forest restoration, habitat conservation and livelihood improvement activities. These activities will address local drivers of deforestation and forest degradation, enabling the project to generate GHG emission reductions, enhance biodiversity and benefit local communities. The project does not intend to produce any carbon credits and is not a carbon project.
ccb-4761:
The REDD+ Estrela Acapuzinho Project seeks the conservation of forests located in the indigenous territories (Terra Indigena) of Acapuri de Cima, Estrela da Paz and Riozinho. located within the municipalities of Fonte Boa, Jutai and Juruá, in the Amazon state of Brazil. The project area has a total extension of 65,452 ha. The territories of these communities are part of the northern geographic area of the country characterized for its high biodiversity and rain tropical forests and for the presence of deforestation activities and social conflicts. Acapuri de Cima consists of 1 indigenous community (Aldeia), Estrela da Paz of 7 and Riozinho of 4. 

In the last years, it has been a national concern the high deforestation rates and associated social and biodiversity impacts in this region. No natural areas were drained or deforested before project beginning to generate carbon credits. Local understanding of the REDD+ mechanism consist in that the more standing forest that their territory maintains, more benefits will be delivered by the project. Deforestation drivers include mining activities, subsistence agriculture, and activities of illegal use. Social issues include absence of the state and lack of sanitation, energy, education and health infrastructure and lack of technical guidance regarding sustainable production models.

The project aims to mitigate the effects caused by climate change by reducing CO2 emissions derived from deforestation and forest degradation, restore degraded forest lands, promote sustainable management of forests, and develop productive activities to improve community welfare. The project also seeks to protect biodiversity and high conservation values, enhance ecological connectivity and secure natural habitats of vulnerable species (including those within some category of threat and those that represent ecological interest.
ccb-4765: Yabu Ala Improved Grassland Management Project (hereinafter referred to as “the project”) is located in Alashan Right Banner, Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region of China. The project is aimed to improve the rotation of grazing animals, limit the timing and number of grazing animals on degraded pastures, and restore degraded land by replanting with grasses and ensuring appropriate management over the long-term. The project proponent is Inner Mongolia Cili Agricultural Development Co., Ltd., Forestry and Animal Husbandry Ecological Technology Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as the Project Proponent or PP). According to the baseline survey, before the implementation of the project, the grassland in the region has experienced serious degradation and even desertification due to the impact of climate change and human activities. Totally, 371,697.88 ha of degraded grassland has been managed properly and there are three main restoration measures namely rest grazing and rotational grazing implemented in moderate degraded area and the categorization is in line with Parameters for Degradation, Sandification and Salification of rangelands (GB19377-2003) .
ccb-4770: The Xinjiang Fuyun Improved Grassland Management Project aims to restore 332,660 hectares of degraded grasslands in Fuyun by adopting a variety of measures, including grazing prohibition and grass planting. The project will increase carbon sequestration, reverse grassland degradation, contribute to local development and preserve cultural traditions. The implementation of the project will significantly improve the local climate benefits, community benefits, and biodiversity benefits.
ccb-4771: The Xinjiang Kalamaili Improved Grassland Management Project  aims to restore 333,346.7 hectares of degraded grasslands in Fuyun by grazing prohibition. The project will increase carbon sequestration, reverse grassland degradation, contribute to local development and preserve cultural traditions.The implementation of the project will significantly improve the local climate benefits, community benefits, and biodiversity benefits.
ccb-4773:
The Vencedor Guajoya REDD+ project is aimed at reducing and preventing GHG emissions from deforestation activities in the forests present in the territory of the Native Community located in the basin and right bank of the Napo River, through the development and implementation of a REDD+ strategy built in a collective and participatory manner with community members and that is also aligned with the objectives of the life plan, which is conceived as a community planning instrument that contains the worldview, history and future vision of community. Likewise, the territorial planning and environmental protection instruments of the region are taken into account.
Within the framework of the development and implementation of the project, the intervention strategy consists of the execution of actions framed in four main components: i) strengthening governance; ii) development of sustainable productive activities compatible with the conservation of biodiversity; iii) increase in social investment; iv) monitoring. This is how the REDD+ project strategy also seeks to integrate different interventions in the territory, by offering economic resources that can potentiate processes in progress or to be implemented and that in turn allows attracting greater investment to the territory for the benefit of the communities.
ccb-4780:
The Sichuan Ganluo IFM (conversion of logged to protected forest) Project (hereafter “the project activity”) is implemented in the Liangshan Yi Autonomous Prefecture and the Ganzi Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture, Sichuan Province of China by Chengdu Haisha Technology Co.,Ltd.. The project is located in two autonomous prefectures. The geographic coordinate  is 102°27′~103°32′ E and 28°28′~29°18′ N and 101°07′~102°16′ E and 28°09′~29°20′ N respectively. The total area is 894,128 ha, which includes the Improved Forest Management (IFM) of the forests in the conversion of logged to protected forest.
The area of the project activity is 4321.92 ha, including 450 subcompartments. The ownership and the right to use the forest land belongs to Ganluo County Xincai Forestry Plantation Co. and Jiulong County Jutiantai Forestry Development Co.. They signed Project Development Cooperation Agreement with Chengdu Haisha Technology Co.,Ltd. (hereafter referred as the project proponent). It authorized the project proponent to use the land for the forest management. The species involved in the project are Liquidambar formosana Hance, Masson Pine, soft broadleaved species, Taxodiaceae, hard broadleaved species and PopulusL. These are common local tree species.
Prior to the implementation of the project activity, the trees are logged annually according to a valid and verifiable government-approved timber management plan for harvesting the project area. The implementation of the project activity converses the trees to protected forest to reduce the GHG emissions for about 1,377,720 tCO2e in 30 years, the average annual emission reduction is 45,924 tCO2e and Verified Carbon Units with buffer deduction is about 1,074,617 tCO2e in 30 years, the average annual VCUs with buffer deduction is 35,821 tCO2e.
ccb-4796: The Cachoeira Porteira Conservation Project is located within the Brazilian Amazon, specifically in Oriximiná municipality in the Pará State, Brazil. The project zone, Cachoeira Porteira territory, has 225,289.53 hectares while the project area encompasses 178,450.77 hectares. Cachoeira Porteira, a remnant quilombo community, is represented by AMOCREQ-CPT, one of the project proponents. Systemica Inteligência em Sustentabilidade S.A is the other project proponent. The Cachoeira Porteira Conservation Project falls under the category of Improved Forest Management. The project activity is Logged to Protected Forest (LtPF), and it utilizes the VM0010 v.1.3 methodology. Therefore, the project shall reduce emissions and combat decreased carbon stocks by conserving the area that would be subject to planned timber harvest in the baseline scenario. The project´s crediting period is 30 years, commencing on November 7th, 2022, and it is expected to be concluded on November 6th, 2052. The estimated average net GHG emission reductions is 567,544.43 tCO2e per year, totaling 17,026,332.88 tCO2e, over the crediting period. It is noteworthy that the Cachoeira Porteira Conservation Project meets the gold level criteria for, climate, community, and biodiversity. In a comprehensive approach, seven activities have been meticulously planned, which are synergistic with the Sustainable Development Goals, including Zero Hunger, Good Health and Well-being, Quality Education, Clean Water and Sanitation, Affordable and Clean Energy, Decent Work and Economic Growth, Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure, Reduced Inequalities, and Life on Land.
ccb-4802:
The Rio Muru REDD+ Project is a grouped project developed by Angelim Participações S.A. that aims to mitigate climate change by reducing greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from planned and unplanned deforestation along the Muru River in Acre state, Brazil. The first project activity instance with 4,883 ha is part of a property of 30,881 hectares with mostly Open Ombrophilous Forest. It will avoid 2,075,259.83tCO2e of GHG emissions over 6 years by curbing planned deforestation. Additional instances in the Project Zone, covering the prevention of both planned and unplanned deforestation, will be incorporated into the project. 

The Project Proponent works with local families to create opportunities for employment and alternative activities to cattle ranching and slash and burn subsistence agriculture. The region also has high species diversity, including Rare, Threatened and Endangered (RTE) species such as Geoffroy’s Wooly Monkey Lagothrix lagotricha cana, Black Spider Monkey Ateles chamek, Big-leaf Mahogany Swietenia macrophylla and Ipê Amarelo Handroanthus serratifolius, among others. The Project aims to improve their conservation status by protecting and restoring their habitat and curbing harmful activities.
ccb-4834:
The Seringal Rio Branco REDD+ Project is a partnership between Biofílica Ambipar Environmental Investments S/A and Amazônia Agroindústria EIRELI, with the aim of promoting forest conservation and mitigating climate change by reducing greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from changes in land use. In addition to the climate benefits, the project also aims to generate socio-environmental benefits based on sustainable economic development practices and improving the well-being of the surrounding communities, while preserving the culture and traditions of the local people.
The Seringal Rio Branco REDD+ Project is located in the Alto Juruá region, between the municipalities of Cruzeiro do Sul and Porto Walter, covering an area of 29,615 hectares. The Juruá River Basin is made up of four micro-basins: the igarapé do meio micro-basin, the igarapé primeiro de março micro-basin and the igarapé grande micro-basin, as well as the Valparaiso River basin (micro-basin), which is the main drainage network in the rubber plantation region.
The region is recognized as one of Brazil's Ramsar Sites, due to its international significance in terms of ecology, botany, zoology, limnology and hydrology. The Seringal Rio Branco REDD+ Project area is of extreme importance for biological conservation, as it is home to a high diversity of fauna and flora, including the presence of endemic and rare species such as the Macuru-papa-mosca bird (Micromonacha lanceolata), which  was recorded for the first time in the state of Acre, in the project area. In addition, the region is home to numerous species that are bioindicators of preserved forest in the Amazon.
ccb-4841: Ana Primavesi is an initiative to support the ecological transition in the Atlantic Forest and Cerrado biomes in Brazil. The grouped project has the target of implementing 2 000 hectares of agroforestry and forest restoration over degraded land with small to medium landowners. Supporting agroecological networks and supply-chains, as well as strengthen income and participation of  women and youth. The project will also catalyze natural resources conservation of soil, water and biodiversity, essential for maintenance of life and food security. The program honours a remarkable scientist who inspired the project’s name. Born in Austria in 1920, she was one of the few women at that time to have the title of Agronomist. She moved to Brazil in 1948 where she dedicated her professional and personal life for ‘ecological agriculture’ (agroecology) studies, becoming a pioneer in the country. She taught in Brazilian Universities and became known for her dedication for soil science and its contribution for food production and nature resilience. Primavesi has written many books and inspired many scientists and farm producers. Her legacy teaches about the importance of learning and respecting natural resources as living organisms, nature laws and processes.
ccb-4847:
The Timor-Leste Mangrove Restoration Project, led by SK Forest Co. Ltd., is focused on restoring degraded mangrove ecosystems along the coast of Timor-Leste. The initial phase of the project will cover 500 hectares across seven municipalities, including Dili, Bobonaro, Baucau, Manatuto, Viqueque, Manufahi, and Cova-Lima, addressing the significant loss of approximately 80% of the nation's mangrove cover since 1940. This degradation is attributed to factors such as sedimentation, sea-level rise, animal grazing, aquaculture, and wood extraction.
The core activity involves planting native mangrove species like Rhizophora apiculata, Avicennia marina, Ceriops tagal, and Sonneratia sp., with species selection adapted to the unique ecological conditions of each site, such as hydrology and salinity. The primary objective is to enhance blue carbon sequestration in both biomass and soil, leading to a net removal of atmospheric greenhouse gases. The project is anticipated to sequester approximately 282,937 tCO2e over a 40-year period, which translates to an average of 7,073 tCO2e per year.
In addition to its climate mitigation benefits, the project is designed to provide significant ecological and social co-benefits. These include improved coastal protection against erosion and storms, enhancement of local biodiversity, and support for community livelihoods through employment in restoration and monitoring activities, as well as capacity-building initiatives.
ccb-4852: The objective of the project is to restore degraded Van Panchayat forests across 160 villages in the Himalayan state of Uttarakhand. The Van Panchayat system in mountain districts of Uttarakhand is a unique system of community led forest management system that recognizes traditional and customary rights of forest dwelling communities
ccb-4854:
The Puno region is located in the southeast of Peru, bordered to the north by the department of Madre de Dios, to the east by Bolivia (Department of La Paz), to the southwest by the departments of Tacna and Moquegua and to the west by the departments of Arequipa and Cusco.
The Puno region is located in the high plateau between 3,812 and 5,500 m above sea level. n. m. and between the jungle fringe and the high jungle between 4,200 and 500 m above sea level. n. m.

The REDD + project is implemented in the area corresponding to the protected natural area of the Bahuaja Sonene National Park in the Puno region. It has an area of 773,345.82 hectares and its objective is to conserve the ANP forest in the face of threats of deforestation and degradation, conserve biodiversity stocks and improve the living conditions of the population surrounding the project area.

The project proposes to reduce the pressure to change land use in the project area through 9 components: control and surveillance, biological monitoring, restoration of degraded areas, physical demarcation of the limits of the ANP, promotion of research, promotion of sustainable productive activities, strengthening of participatory management, dissemination and environmental education, implementation of environmental and social safeguards.

With these actions, the project expects to avoid a total of 1,111,430 tCO2-e according to the base scenario projected for the first 10 years, with an average annual net emissions of 111,143 tCO2-e. In addition, the project includes benefits for the populations involved, as well as for the conservation of biodiversity, where it seeks to contribute to the conservation of forests with high levels of biodiversity with the presence of endemic species, species in danger of extinction or to some degree. threat, beyond the benefits of reducing GHG emissions.
ccb-4857: The AWA REDD+ Project has an area of 66,443.13 hectares, belonging to the Associação dos Remanescentes de Quilombos de Gurupá (ARQMG), which is home to 12 quilombo communities in the municipality of Gurupá, Pará. The business as usual consists in slash-and-burn agriculture for cassava cultivation, a traditional practice adopted by the quilombolas, and  deforestation followed by sale of timber and implementation of pasture for cattle raising, especially near the municipalities of Gurupá and Porto de Moz. Through various actions, the project will promote forest conservation and reduce GHG emissions that would occur due to deforestation, without harming the traditional and cultural practices of the communities, such as remote satellite monitoring, ground patrolling, fire brigade trainings, trainings in good agricultural practices, delimitation and signaling of the boundaries, among others. Furthermore, the project will promote the socio-economic and environmental development. To achieve these results, four programs will be implemented in the territory: I) Territorial Management, II) Socio-bio-economic Development, III) Promotion of Community Citizenship and IV) Biodiversity Conservation. These programs, as well as their benefits and impacts, were defined and identified with the 12 communities of the territory. The definition, identification and evaluation method used participatory workshops, respecting the principles of ILO Convention 169.
ccb-4858: The Nkuba REDD+ Project (NRP) is designed to promote climate change mitigation, preserve biodiversity, and establish alternative livelihoods for communities through the UN-REDD+ framework. The NRP is expected to reduce an average of 256,808 t CO2e per year, The Project Zone is 105,572 ha and covers the Nkuba Conservation Area (NCA), located in North Kivu & Maniema provinces, DRC. The NRP consists mainly of primary rainforest including numerous unique species. The NCA landscape is dominated by plains, plateaus, and low mountains above small marshy valleys. It has numerous rivers and tributaries with conditions for a thriving tropical ecosystem.  The NRP consists of three forest blocks that are recognised by the Congolese authorities as community forest conservation concessions (CFCLs). The CFCLs involved in the NRP are Mbungu, Nsuhu, and Seko, with a total of six clans making up the project communities. The benefits of the NRP forest are significant, but the region continues to experience threats due to deforestation, uncontrolled hunting, artisanal mining, and nomadic activities. The lack of employment, business opportunities, limited access to infrastructure and basic services contribute to local populations exploiting the forest for income generation. In response to these threats to the NCA, the 6 clans in partnership with Dian Fossey Gorilla Fund created NRP with the following objectives: 1) Mitigate climate change caused by deforestation and degradation and develop adaptation strategies for climate variability, 2) Improve the quality of life for local communities by introducing sustainable alternatives to forest exploitation, income-generating activities, and initiatives designed to address community needs, such as health, education, and safety, 3) Contribute to preserving biodiversity through community-led forest management, better land strategies, and forest monitoring, regulation, and surveillance.
ccb-4860: The grouped project’s aim is to undertake agroforestry on fallow/ degraded lands of the individual smallholder farmers holding 0.2 to 1 ha of land in Jharkhand, India, through the establishment of horticultural trees yielding fruits, and timber based agroforestry model and by intercropping of seasonal crops in the farmers plot. The first instance consists of afforestation of 5000 hectare (ha) of fallow lands owned by local smallholder farmers that are lying unutilized for decades owing to various reasons such as lack of financial resources, migrant labor, etc. The project entails the planting of a variety of native species depending primarily on the soil types and local (market) demand, in consultation with the community members, for example, timber yielding trees comprising Teak (Tectona Grandis) and fruit yielding types including Mango (Mangifera Indica), Guava (Psidium guajava), Orange (Citrus Sinensis), among other species. To ensure the longevity and sustainability of the project, it will be managed by the local community. The activities under the project will contribute to multiple indicators for the Sustainable Development Goals such as No poverty (SDG 1), Zero Hunger (SDG 2), Gender Equality (SDG 5), Clean Water and Sanitation (SDG 6), Decent Work and Economic Growth (SDG 9), Climate Action (SDG 13), Life on Land (SDG 15).  The overall goal of the project is to, through afforestation activities, recover and utilize fallow lands and to promote connectivity between ecosystems by providing pathways for wildlife, facilitating movement and genetic exchange between fragmented habitats. In addition the project is majorly focused on enhancing livelihoods of the local communities in the project area. Marginal farmers in Jharkhand suffer from low income due to low productivity due to existing issues such as less fertile land, less use of manure, greater dependence on monsoons, backward/ outdated and limited technology, and unproductive use of debt.
ccb-4865:
The OGA REDD+ PROJECT aims to protect 8,348.78 hectares of Amazon rainforest located in Machadinho d’Oeste municipalitiy, Rondônia State, Brazil. The project promotes forest conservation and estimates to reduce 1,884,762.84 tCO2e (average of 62,825.43 tCO2e/year) in 30 years by Avoiding Unplanned Deforestation (AUD) and Avoiding Planned Deforestation (APD) in Lote 11 property.
AUD PAI scenario: The state of Rondônia has been expressive in the expansion of the Brazilian agricultural frontier, being agriculture and livestock the central axes of its economy. In 2023 the state saw a 450% increase in deforestation, being the third state with the highest deforestation contributions in the Legal Amazon. In Machadinho d’Oeste, this expansion led to increase in illegal deforestation, mainly for livestock, also resulting in the increase of social conflicts and illegal invasions. Furthermore, it is common for private properties in the region to exceed the conversion limit (or legal deforestation) allowed by the Forest Code. The main factors that lead producers to deforest their properties beyond the limit established in the Forest Code, according to various scientific studies, are (i) the opportunity cost of conserving the forest or native vegetation and (ii) the state's lack of supervision.
APD PAIs scenario: The project area is in compliance with the Forest Code, and the proponents will waive their right to legal suppression in order to protect the standing forest, thus avoiding an economically driven planned deforestation activity.
Given project approval, measures/technologies such as fire brigade training (internal and external community), reinforcement of terrestrial and remote monitoring, training courses will be carried out to qualify the project's employees and neighbours among other social activities will be implemented.
ccb-4867:
The AHU REDD+ Project conserves 32,326.6 ha of unique transitional forests between the Cerrado and Amazon biomes (CAT). The Project takes place in the Agrochapada farm, municipality of Paranatinga, State of Mato Grosso, Brazil. The without project scenario is illegal logging is followed by frequent fire events.  Fire is used as a tool for deforestation. It spreads quickly in the draught season and causes degradation and extinction of forest patches.
The project employs protective technologies grouped under a Forest Integrity Program and preventive measures carried out under a Community Network Program. By doing so, it will avoid 9,164 hectares of modelled deforestation in four different phytophysiognomies. The total GHG emission reduction expected throughout the project´s 30 years 1,090,225.29 tCO2, with an annual average of 35,168.56 tCO2.
As part of the CCB Standard, the objectives for climate, community and biodiversity during the project life cycle are as follows:
Climate: a) To effectively prevent and control forest fires in and around the project area; and b) To effectively prevent deforestation and improve monitoring in and around the project area.
Community:a) Increase income opportunities for women; b) Increase the thermal comfort; c) To increase opportunities for physical activities; d) Enhance preventive health measures; and e) To improve education for the internal community at all levels.
Biodiversity: a) To reduce the impact of human activities on biodiversity; b)To improve the effectiveness of the farm´s restoration actions.
ccb-4872: The grouped project’s aim is to undertake afforestation in fallow lands in the districts of Alipurduar, Jalpaiguri and Cooch Behar in West Bengal, India, through the establishment of horticultural (trees yielding fruits, flowers, medicines, fodder, etc.) and timber plantations. The first instance consists of afforestation of 5000 hectare (ha) of fallow lands owned by local smallholder farmers, that are lying unutilized for decades owing to various reasons such as human-animal conflicts, floods, lack of financial resources, etc. The project entails the planting of a variety of native species depending primarily on the soil types and local (market) demand, in consultation with the community members, whereby the first instance of plantation will be carried out across 3 (three) years. For example, timber yielding trees will comprise Gamhar (Gmelina Arborea) and Arjuna (Terminalia Arjuna) and fruit yielding types will include Jackfruit (Artocarpus heterophyllus) and Jamun (Syzygium Cumini), among other species. Through afforestation activities to recover fallow lands, the project aims to promote connectivity between ecosystems and enhance livelihoods of the local communities. In addition, this project is expected to provide more than 200 full-time employment opportunities (with equal access to women and men) in a zone historically affected by poverty.
ccb-4881: Since its inception in 1999, over 200,000 participants organized into over 31,000 TIST Small Groups have planted over 25 million trees in Tanzania, India, Kenya, and Uganda - accomplishing GhG sequestration through tree planting, creating a potential long-term income stream, and developing sustainable environments and livelihoods. Tanzania 011 is a subset of the TIST project in Tanzania and applies to 638 Small Groups, 3,740 Participants, 2,611 active Project Areas, and 2,882 hectares.  TIST farmers use a mosaic restoration approach, planting on thousands of individual farms spread across the landscape. The individual farms are found throughout Tanzania and concentrated around Mpwapwa and Kibondo.
ccb-4890: The Regenerative Development of Anlo Wetlands Project is a grouped project that aims to help adapt to climate change, enhance biodiversity and ecosystem health, and improve livelihoods of communities dependent on the local mangrove ecosystem. With a potential for expansion of planting up to 9,991 hectares of mangrove in the Keta Lagoon in Ghana, the first instance covers approximately 1,536 hectares. The primary objective of the project is to expand the mangrove area through the planting of diverse native mangrove species. This aims to enhance the positive functions and ecosystem services that mangroves provide to communities and biodiversity. The project is situated in the Volta region, within the Keta Lagoon Complex Ramsar site. This site is recognised for its exceptional biodiversity and wetland ecosystems and faces a necessity of preservation. Thus, the project's location contributes to enhancing the health and connectivity of habitats and ecosystems. The project is led by Terraformation as the project proponent, with the Regenerative Development of Anlo Wetlands Foundation as the project implementer of the project activities. The project activities will take place in locations selected based on their ecological suitability, in collaboration with local communities. The project design encourages and promotes active participation from these local communities. The project plans to reverse mangrove decline, restore ecosystem services, and offer sustainable livelihood opportunities while preserving biodiversity. The project will achieve these aims through large-scale mangrove reforestation, regenerative aquaculture, and apiculture. In addition to restoring native vegetation and habitat for fish and wildlife, the project will generate GHG benefits by sequestering carbon dioxide from the atmosphere through the restoration of mangrove ecosystems.
ccb-4906:
The project aim is to protect and restore forests within designated Social Forestry areas in Kapuas Hulu district, West Kalimantan, Indonesia, for which local communities have secured management rights for a period of 35-years; to prevent greenhouse gas emissions, increase forest carbon stocks, conserve biodiversity, maintain and enhance ecosystem services, and improve local livelihoods; the project has the following climate, community, and biodiversity objectives:
The project’s Climate Objective is to reduce GHG emissions from deforestation and forest degradation by protecting and conserving Social Forestry areas in Kapuas Hulu district. 
Its Community Objective is to improve community prosperity in villages in Kapuas Hulu that have secured ownership or management rights through Indonesia’s Social Forestry program by improving forest-based economic values and sustainable agriculture practices.
The project’s Biodiversity Objective is to protect and conserve biodiversity within Social Forestry areas in Kapuas Hulu district and to maintain and enhance habitat extent and quality for threatened species.
ccb-4915:
The Mafisa Livestock Grazing Carbon Project (MLGCP) is proposed by ZayoHub, a Zambian non-profit. The project aims to generate carbon credits through enhanced grazing and fire management, utilizing VM0032 methodology, (Adoption of Sustainable Grasslands through Adjustment of Fire & Grazing). It will monitor activities and impacts through on-the-ground livestock tracking by grazing coordinators and via remote impact assessment via satellite imagery. 

The initiative focuses on empowering impoverished local communities residing in mopane and miombo woodlands in southwestern Zambia. In this region, soils are poor; farming is largely subsistence-based and highly marginal, and cattle rearing is the dominant historical land use. Key aspects of long-standing traditional farming practices reflect the principles of rotational grazing and good fire management, but their use has lapsed in recent decades. 

Improving animal husbandry on sustainably managed rangelands is a significant opportunity for sustainable livelihoods in the project area. However, at present animals are usually not herded, contributing to degradation of grassland degradation. High tick-borne disease prevalence and other parasites greatly impede productivity. 

MLGCP promotes cattle grazing rotations to restore traditional grazing practices, simulate wild herbivores' migratory patterns, and foster grassland regeneration. Additionally, it targets the reduction of burning frequency, enhancing carbon storage. MLGCP will provide animal health services for farmers participating in collective planned grazing. 

Anticipating annual net removals of 1 ton of CO2e/ha, the project plans to expand from 220,000 ha initially to 1.26 million ha by 2030. Projected annual carbon credit yields are set to rise from 220,000 tons CO2e in 2024 to around 1.26 million tons CO2e by 2029, sustaining until 2063. Overall, MLGCP aims to remove over 47 million tons CO2e, contributing to long-term atmospheric carbon reduction.
ccb-4924: This project features implementation of rapid rotational grazing practices by dense aggregations of livestock to restore perennial grasses on degraded rangelands across 970,685 hectares in northern Tanzania. These new grazing practices are additional because they differ from the currently practiced seasonal shifts in grazing activity from wet to dry season ranges, and the new practices would not be possible without carbon revenues to support governance and monitoring of grazing activities. Rapid rotational grazing will enhance adaptation to climate change by improving soil water holding capacity, increasing surface water availability and providing grass banks as a hedge against drought. Habitat improvement from new grazing practices will result in biodiversity benefits in the form of improved habitat inside wildlife corridors between iconic High Conservation Areas such as Serengeti, Kilimanjaro, Nairobi, and Tsavo National Parks and their associated ecosystems and enhance diversity of endemic taxa of plants, birds and insects. Finally, the project will provide direct benefits to dozens of pastoralist communities in form of funds for bursaries to support women and the poorest community members as well as to construct water capture structures and infrastructure for delivering livestock to market. The project is expected to remove more than 62 million tons CO2e over the project lifetime of 40 years, or more than 1.5 million tons CO2e a year on average.
ccb-4956:
The Tapera Amazonas REDD+ Project in Urucará and Nhamundá, Amazonas, Brazil, combats severe deforestation. Amazonas experienced considerable forest loss, with 4,913 km² deforested in 2021 and 2,741 km² in 2022, leading to high CO2 emissions. Main causes include illegal logging, cattle ranching, and agriculture expansion. Urucará and Nhamundá, however, maintain high forest coverage, emphasizing their ecological importance. The project focuses on conservation, biodiversity protection, and sustainable practices.

Deforestation drivers in these areas are illegal logging and agricultural expansion, with Urucará particularly affected due to timber industries in nearby São Sebastião. The project, under the Verified Carbon Standard (VCS) for Forestry, aims to reduce emissions from deforestation and degradation. It plans to improve monitoring, employ new staff for farm management, and use carbon credits for environmental and social enhancements.

In line with Brazil's Forest Code, the project supports maintaining 80% of forest cover in the Legal Amazon. Community benefits include water systems, solar panels, satellite internet, and training for sustainable forest product processing. A processing factory in Urucará will offer alternative income sources. Operations are expected to start in January 2025. The project is significant for biodiversity, located within a Key Biodiversity Area, home to unique and endangered species. It prioritizes ecosystem functions like nutrient cycling and carbon sequestration. Monitoring will involve satellite imagery, drone-based techniques, and fire prevention strategies, focusing on conserving forest areas against legal deforestation pressures.
ccb-4966: The REDD+ project is called Yambone, which in Yao, the local dialect, means 'To Make Better'. The project aims to improve various aspects of the Chipanje Chetu area in the northern part of Sanga district. The main objective is the conservation of the miombo forest, a complicated and delicate ecosystem that is the victim of illegal deforestation by farmers and charcoal burners. In addition, the project aims to improve the existence of the five local communities, helping them to develop as sustainable a path as possible, accompanying them in various areas, from improving agriculture to health, from access to energy to education. The project area covers a large area, 6500 square kilometres, and to protect it, the help of the community is needed, part of which will be taken on by the project and will be an integral part of it. The Yambone project is designed to be developed as a traditional carbon project, with the addition of specific actions and monitoring of the community and biodiversity components. Thus, not only will the carbon contained in the area and related risks be estimated and quantified, but also specific activities for some particularly fragile community categories will be implemented and improved over time, and animal and plant species of particular importance to the ecosystem will be identified and then watched over and monitored, demonstrating that the project will bring benefits in this respect as well. Objectives In summary, the main objectives of the Yambone REDD+ project are therefore as follows: • protection of forest and carbon stocks against illegal deforestation • community development, focusing on sustainable practices • biodiversity enhancement, using the presence and behaviour of key species as a proxy Finally, the Yambone REDD+ project is designed to be replicable and scalable, annexing neighbouring areas in the near future. Assessing the minimum requirements of neighbouring areas to be annexed to the project,
ccb-4967: The PLUM Peat and Mangrove Conservation and Restoration Project (PLUM Project) is a conservation and restoration project of peat and mangrove forests located in Central Kalimantan Province, Indonesia. The project is implemented on a 23,665-hectare forest concession with Forest Utilization Business License (PBPH). Prior to the PLUM Project, the project area was legally authorized and documented to be converted into oil palm plantation. The project’s goal is to conserve the remaining forest, restore ecosystem function, protect biodiversity, and improve the well-being of communities to become resilient to climate change. The project proponent will implement activities to maximize the positive impact of the project for the climate, community and biodiversity. Forest protection activities such as forest patrols, fire prevention, construction of fire towers and guard posts and regular monitoring of biodiversity will be implemented to prevent forest loss and protect biodiversity. Peat ecosystems will be restored by blocking canals to rewet the area and avoid further peat drainage. Furthermore, the project will rehabilitate a total of 15,088 ha degraded land, composed of 424 ha of ARR in mangrove, 1,306 ha of ARR on peatland, and 13,358 ha of Assisted Natural Regeneration on peat. The project will provide tangible benefits to local communities living in the surrounding area by working to improve local livelihoods, health, education, and well-being. The project area is home to 31 globally threatened species, including the Bornean orangutan, Proboscis monkey, and the Bornean white-bearded gibbon. The project activities will contribute to the conservation of these species and their habitat, and restore the degraded peatland and mangroves to improve the habitat quality and reduce the threats to biodiversity.

The NRP is expected to reduce an average of 256,808 t CO2e per year, The Project Zone is 105,572 ha and covers the Nkuba Conservation Area (NCA), located in North Kivu & Maniema provinces, DRC. ccb-4985: OYU Green's Greening India Mission (GIM) is a multifaceted grouped project, targeting large-scale reforestation in 5,000 hectares of dormant lands in Assam, India. With farmers and landowners at the forefront, GIM focuses on long-term carbon dioxide removal by establishing plantation of locally preferred tree species, promotes sustainable land use, creates income and employment opportunities, enhances digital literacy, and strengthens community resilience to climate change. By restoring habitats and creating wildlife corridors, the project also safeguards local biodiversity in this globally recognized biodiversity hotspot.
ccb-5027:
In the Eastern and Western Cape Provinces of South Africa, livestock overgrazing has played a significant role in desertification within the Subtropical Thicket Biome (STB), also known as the Albany Thicket Biome. Approximately 90% of the biome has experienced moderate to severe degradation as a result. This degradation has had detrimental impacts on critical ecosystem functions, including reduced availability of forage, increased soil erosion and runoff, decreased soil fertility and productivity, compromised water retention capacity, and loss of habitats. Consequently, farmers and agricultural workers have been experiencing declines in their livelihoods as the land can support progressively fewer animals.
The main objective of the project is to restore the functionality of 100,000 ha of degraded areas within the STB by reintroducing spekboom (Portulacaria afra), a pivotal species recognized for its effectiveness in thicket restoration. across the municipalities of the Eastern and Western Cape Provinces of South Africa, covering regions where the STB naturally occurs. The restoration efforts are expected to have far-reaching benefits, including carbon sequestration, biodiversity recovery, and improved livelihoods for participating landowners and communities.
ccb-5041:
The project aims to support efforts to protect and improve social forestry management and governance in three village forests. The project’s climate, community and biodiversity objectives are summarized below. 
Climate Objective: Reduce emissions from deforestation and forest degradation by improving Village Forest governance and management.
Biodiversity Objective: Conserve biodiversity by protecting HCV areas, rehabilitating degraded areas of the Village Forest and preventing activities that damage biodiversity in the Village Forest.
Community Objective: Improve community wellbeing through the development of sustainable Non-Timber Forest Products (NTFP), agricultural commodities and other sources of income.
ccb-5061:
This project aims to restore 30,000 hectares of degraded pasture that has been historically cleared for cattle grazing in the Provinces of Guanacaste, San Jose & Puntarenas in Costa Rica. A total of 7,500+ hectares will be reforested, focusing on riparian areas, which will create wildlife corridors to improve biodiversity, and the remaining 22,500 hectares will be transitioned to rotational grazing systems, which will restore ecosystem services and income streams for the participating ganaderos. The 30,000ha project area will comprise a mosaic of privately owned farmland.
The project is comprised of three core interventions:
1.	Reforestation (VM0047) – An accelerator approach to reforestation using pioneer species to provide shade for mid- and late-stage succession species will be implemented on 7,500+ hectares of pasture that has previously been converted from forest. Reforestation will primarily focus on restoring riparian areas and water ecosystem services, which will encourage project permanence, as water is a precious resource in these drought prone areas. 
2.	Rotational Grazing Programme (VM0042) – Ganaderos will be provided with training, equipment and ongoing guidance to transition remaining pasture into more sustainable and productive rotational grazing systems. 
3.	Community Development Strategy and Sustainable Business and Livelihood Fund (SBLF) - Funds generated from carbon credit revenues will be accumulated in the SBLF and be disbursed as a combination of direct payments and sustainable investment finance to further improve profitability and sustainability. Investments may be made at the discretion of the ganaderos into community programmes and local services. 


This project represents a climate adaptation for participating ganaderos by building environmental and financial resilience and is estimated to sequester 5,277,251.77CO2e over the 40-year project period.
ccb-5063: The Delta Blue Carbon Project – Phase 2 (DBC-2) is a public-private partnership initiative of Government of Sindh, Caelum Environmental Solutions and Pollination to promote climate change mitigation and adaptation, conserve and sustainable manage marine and coastal biodiversity, contribute to the achievement of various sustainable development goals and achieve women’s empowerment in the Project Zone12.The Project Zone is an area of 250,000 ha of the Sindh Indus Delta Region in Sujawal and Badin districts of Sindh Province in south-eastern Pakistan. The delta is a vast complex of tidal river channels and creeks, low-lying islands, mangrove forests and inter-tidal areas. The delta’s mangrove forests are unique in being the largest area of arid-climate mangroves in the world.
ccb-5077:
The SEIKOPAI REDD+ project aims to reduce and prevent GHG emissions from deforestation activities in the territory of the Native Community located in the basin and right bank of the Napo River, at Santa Maria stream, through the development and implementation of a REDD+ strategy built collectively and in a participatory manner with the members of the community and also aligned with the objectives of the life plan, which is conceived as a communal planning instrument that contains the worldview, history and vision of the community. It also takes into account the territorial planning and environmental protection instruments of the region to articulate the REDD+ strategy. 

This project corresponds to the Agriculture, Forestry and Other Land Use (AFOLU) sector, in the category of Reducing Emissions from Deforestation and Forest Degradation (REDD+). The project area is within the community territory and covers 134.228 ha of amazon humid forest. It is expected to avoid the emission of 8.780.025 tCO2 for 40 years, which corresponds to 219.500 tCO2/year. Aboveground Biomass (BA of trees and non-trees), Belowground Biomass (BS) and Soil Organic Carbon (COS) pools are taken into account in the project's carbon accounting, considering them to estimate the baseline scenario and monitor performance during project implementation.

During the last years, this amazon area has been under threat due to logging, agricultural expansion and fauna exploitation. Mining is also increasing in surrounding areas, thus representing a huge threat to the ecosystem’s conservation. The project aims to tackle forest pressures and contribute to mitigate climate change by reducing CO2 emissions derived from deforestation, restore degraded lands, promote sustainable management of forests and develop productive activities to improve community welfare. The project seeks to protect biodiversity and high conservation values, maintain ecological connectivity and secure natural habitats for vulnerable and threatened species along with other biodiversity of cultural and spiritual importance for the communities.  

The climate, community and biodiversity objectives are detailed next:

The climate objective is to mitigate climate change through measures that reduce and prevent deforestation and forest degradation activities. The expected results include decrease in illegal logging, recovery of degraded forests, reduction of forest conversion to other land uses and maintained forest carbon stocks over time.

The community objectives were defined with the members of the Vencedor community and aim to improve their living conditions in the territory and include: i) strengthening governance; ii) development of sustainable productive activities compatible with biodiversity conservation; iii) increase social investment; iv) improve monitoring and biodiversity protection initiatives.

Regarding biodiversity conservation, the project seeks to protect amazon tropical forest and its diversity, contribute to maintain the functional connectivity of this forest areas, improve knowledge and management capacities of productive systems that favour biodiversity, as compared to baseline scenario conditions.

In this way the REDD+ project generates a positive impact since it contributes to improve living conditions of the native communities and protects biodiversity to secure the provision of ecosystem services and ecological structure in the long term.
ccb-5084:
Gannan Improved Grassland Management Project (hereafter as “the project”) is located in Gannan Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture, Gansu Province of China. Gannan Tibetan autonomous prefecture is located in the south of Gansu Province, the junction of Gansu, Qingdao and Sichuan Provinces. The project’s aim is to restore the local degraded grassland ecosystem by seeding grass and building fence on the degraded grassland, increase carbon sequestration and contribute to local development by introducing sustainable grazing and management of grassland.
Totally, 157,153.35 ha of degraded grassland have been managed scientifically by fence building and reseeding of local high-quality forage.
Besides these main restoration measures, the project also alleviates soil desertification and restore grassland vegetation to improve soil carbon storage and local biodiversity through grassland management measures, such as daily management measures from other protect projects like rodent and pest control and grassland fire prevention to ensure the long-term sustainable management of the project area.
ccb-5107:
The TERAKA program is a smallholder reforestation and sustainable development initiative in Madagascar. Inspired by the successful TIST model in East Africa, the program empowers farmers to plant and own trees on their land while receiving training from TERAKA and 70% of carbon benefits. Organized into Small Groups, farmers actively combat deforestation, poverty, and drought through sustainable practices that integrate carbon sequestration. By turning carbon credits into a 'virtual' cash crop, the initiative enhances both environmental and economic resilience.
Currently operating in central and eastern Madagascar, TERAKA aims to scale up across the country, starting with 6,000 hectares in its first phase. This phase is projected to sequester more than two million tonnes of greenhouse gases over 40 years while restoring degraded land, improving local livelihoods, fostering sustainable employment, and promoting biodiversity.
ccb-5131: This Improved Forest Management project is a Logged to Protected Forest (LtPF) project type, located on approximately 33,000 acres of privately-owned land in Southwestern Virginia. The project activity consists of the buy-out of a long-term timber lease and surveillance of the project area.
ccb-5137:
The Grand Katanga Reforestation Project is an Afforestation, Reforestation and Revegetation (ARR) grouped project that aims to restore large areas of degraded land through reforestation of native tree species, including enrichment planting and assisted natural regeneration in the Grand Katanga region of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DR Congo). 
The project proponent, Carbon Ventures Africa (CVA), partners with rural communities that have long-term rights to substantial areas of degraded and deforested land that could benefit from reforestation. The project finances the re-establishment of long-term maintenance and protection of native Miombo woodlands by local communities. In parallel, the project finances complementary investments in the local communities including improved agriculture and the planting of fast-growing species for sustainable charcoal production, thereby addressing the two main causes of deforestation in the region.
The project achieves durable, high-integrity GHG removals through nature-based sequestering of carbon dioxide (CO2), resulting from the net biomass growth in successfully implemented reforestation areas, and establishment of vegetation on degraded forestlands, bare soils, and degraded agricultural lands. The project is also seeking the certification to Climate, Community & Biodiversity (CCB) standards as a result of its positive impacts on climate change, local communities and biodiversity.
ccb-514: Validation achieved to the CCB Standards Second Edition, Biodiversity Gold Level, on 27 February 2014. Gap validation to remove two farms from the project area and verification achieved to the CCB Standards Second Edition, Biodiversity Gold Level on 03 March 2017.  The project will establish rubber tree plantations in a project boundary of 2,366.16 hectares of degraded and degrading lands where the traditional use has been cattle grazing, which corresponds to eligible area. The species planted will be Hevea brasiliensis. Direct planting of H. brasiliensis in the project area began in 2007 and will continue through 2013. The real or effective planted area corresponds to 2,252.23 hectares which is given by planting density of natural rubber plantations.  This area excludes other vegetated areas within project boundary such as creeks, borders’ vegetation, and small spots of vegetation.
ccb-5153: The Kafue-Zambezi Community Forest Project (KZCFP) is a potentially large-scale grouped REDD+ initiative set to be implemented in the watersheds of two of Zambia’s most important rivers: The Zambezi River and the Kafue River in Central-West Zambia. First project activity instances are located in the Western Province, with the project area forming a significant part of the Kavango-Zambezi (KAZA) Trans-Frontier Conservation Area (KAZA TFCA) on the Zambian side. The targeted area for phase one is projected to cover 1.95 million hectares, dependent on community willingness to participate and Government approvals. Implementation will be carried out in collaboration with traditional authorities and the Government of the Republic of Zambia. The project aims to reduce emissions through the implementation of the following mitigation activities: engagement and capacity building with key government and community stakeholders, promotion of alternative and sustainable livelihood activities, direct conservation support as well as performance-based payments to community stakeholders delivered through local institutions.
ccb-5169:
The Sembrando Futuro 2.0 project aims to restore native forests across the Central and Western Andes of Colombia. Designed as a grouped ARR project, its first instance focuses on restoring 555 hectares of degraded lands in the departments of Antioquia, Caldas, and Chocó, with a long-term goal of expanding within the region. Restoration areas span diverse Andean ecosystems—including tropical humid, premontane, low montane, and montane forests—located between 80 and more than 3,100 meters in altitude. These forests have undergone extensive degradation due to agricultural expansion, cattle ranching, and land-use pressures.
The project centers on the recovery of native forests, planting over 70 native species to accelerate ecological succession, improve forest structure, and strengthen connectivity between fragmented habitats. Restoration activities contribute to climate mitigation through increased carbon sequestration and enhanced ecosystem resilience.
Sembrando Futuro 2.0 creates substantial community benefits by generating jobs, strengthening local technical capacity, and improving livelihoods through training and equitable carbon revenue sharing. Participating landowners formalize their commitments through 40-year Conservation Agreements, ensuring long-term forest protection, maintenance responsibilities, and sustained community engagement.
The project promotes biodiversity conservation by restoring habitat within and around areas of high ecological importance and key wildlife corridors. At least eight IUCN-listed plant species are expected to benefit from reduced threats and habitat expansion.
Planting began in September 2023, with the first instance planned for completion in 2025. This initial instance is expected to remove 159,280 tCO₂e over 40 years. Sembrando Futuro 2.0 represents a long-term, scalable effort to restore Andean forest ecosystems, enhance biodiversity, support rural livelihoods, and contribute to national and global climate goals.
ccb-5172:
Rainforest Builder Ltd is an integrated tropical forest restoration company founded in 2022 to pioneer tropical forest ecosystem restoration as a commercial undertaking, by combining the best restoration science with professional forestry industry practice to deliver ecosystem restoration at unprecedented quality and scale. Rainforest Builder’s projects aim to return degraded formerly forested lands to primary levels of biomass, biodiversity and structural complexity rapidly and resiliently, in partnership with a range of stakeholders.

The ARR VCS-CCB project is a grouped project that aims to restore approximately 100,000 ha in degraded Forest Reserves in Ghana. The project aims to achieve the sustainable restoration of highly degraded reserve areas through diversified mixed-species plantings that re-establish native flora and fauna, enhance ecological connectivity, and mitigate the adverse effects of deforestation. Central to this endeavour is the goal of ecosystem restoration, achieved with best-practice planting methods to maximise the survival and growth of indigenous species mixes, using species that are carefully selected to re-create natural forest structure. 

The Climate, Community, and Biodiversity goals of the project are to re-establish and protect natural forest landscapes, recovering threatened biodiversity in a globally important conservation hotspot, sequestering CO2 and improving the provision of ecosystem services including water regulation, nutrient cycling, and climate regulation. The project will provide long-term sustainable employment through reforestation and maintenance activities, promoting economic development and enhancing wellbeing in communities adjacent to project areas.
ccb-5181: Silk Grass Farms is a vertically integrated B-certified agribusiness in Southern Belize, committed to innovating positive environmental and social impact at scale. The farm operates within a 27,500-acre tract of land in Stann Creek, Belize.  Approximately 90% of the land (24,700 acres) is pristine first-growth rainforest, protected in perpetuity by the Silk Grass Wildlife Preserve (SGWP). The remaining 10% of the property (approximately 3,000 acres) was previously cultivated for commercial agriculture using conventional farming methods that eroded the topsoil and decreased biodiversity. Maintaining SGWP is critical to the survival of many species and to protecting the natural ecological processes that keep the landscape healthy. The preserve sits at the northeastern edge of the Chiquibul Maya Mountain Massif, which is among the most intact tropical forests north of the Amazon and accounts for 22.2% of the land mass of Belize. Silk Grass Farms is working alongside expert consultants to develop an Avoided Planned Deforestation project to protect 13,000 acres of forest that would have been converted to agricultural lands in the absence of funding from a carbon project. Financial benefits generated through the project activities will be used to support the goals and operations of Silk Grass Wildlife Preserve.
ccb-5183:
Zhangye Improved Grassland Management Project Phase II (hereafter as “the project”) is located in Zhangye City, Gansu Province of China. The project’s aim is to restore the local degraded grassland ecosystem by seeding grass and building fence on the degraded grassland, increase carbon sequestration and contribute to local development by introducing sustainable grazing and management of grassland.
Totally, 138,293.34 ha of degraded grassland have been managed scientifically by fence building and seeding of local high-quality forage. Besides, the project also alleviates soil desertification and restore grassland vegetation to improve soil carbon storage and local biodiversity through grassland management measures, such as daily management measures from other protect projects like rodent and pest control and grassland fire prevention to ensure the long-term sustainable management of the project area.
ccb-5200:
The goal of Together the Forest Awaeté REDD+ Project is to Avoid Unplanned Deforestation (AUD) of the Parakanã Indigenous Land in Pará, Brazil. Home of 1,500 indigenous people, the Parakanã Land encompasses 351,697.41 hectares of the Amazon Forest situated in the heart of the deforestation arc, with unparalleled biodiversity of flora and fauna.

Parakanã Land is located within the municipalities of Novo Repartimento and Itupiranga, both identified as high-priority areas for the deforestation prevention, monitoring, and control. Between 2009 and 2019, a total of 291,280 hectares were deforested. The Parakanã Land represents the largest contiguous forested area in the region, largely due to the proactive protection efforts of indigenous communities.

Indigenous People play a pivotal role in the conservation of the Amazon Forest. Their land use practices are often more holistic, combining traditional ways of life with modern perspectives on sustainable use. Within the Parakanã community, despite the vast richness of the forest, families grapple with a heightened degree of social vulnerability due to intense pressures from surrounding activities, such as livestock farming and illegal logging.

The Together for the Forest Program aims to rethink the socioeconomic development model of the Amazon region based on fostering bioeconomy value chains. It proposes a blended finance architecture, that finances several activities to prevent deforestation in the short term, while ensures long term permanence through social, infrastructure and local value chains development. The community played a significant role in prioritizing the value chains of bioeconomy products to be promoted and identifying key social priorities.

It is expected to avoid 69,134 hectares of deforestation, reducing an average of annual emission of 1,294,534 tCO2e, and a total of 51,781,360 tCO2e, over the project’s 40-year lifetime.
ccb-5232:
V Carbon Nuku Maimai REDD+ Project (the Nuku Maimai Project) locates in West Sepik (Sandaun) Province, the north-westernmost province of Papua New Guinea. Sandaun Province is comparatively poor. Income-earning opportunities are low across the province. A lack of road infrastructure hinders market access and commercial development in the province. The Nuku Maimai Project covers an area of about 102,779 ha of massive natural forests in a critical region of the threatened biodiversity hotspot of Papua New Guinea.
Some mitigation measures implemented by the Nuku Maimai Project to prevent planned deforestation will be implemented by stepping up local surveillance, mapping local deforestation patterns, forming collaborations with educational and research institutions, and offering advantages to neighbouring communities with the aim of minimizing deforestation by providing alternative income, education, and professional training.
The goal of the Nuku Maimai Project is to help conserving and protecting the natural rainforest within the Maimai Project Area from being cleared and converted as part of the Maimai Integrated Agro Forestry Development Plan. The Nuku Maimai Project’s operations at the Maimai Forest help to safeguard the forest from planned deforestation based on the mechanisms to finance and achieve the Social and Governance (SDG) goals established by the United Nations. 
The forests under the V Carbon Nuku Maimai REDD+ Project will be protected from clearance, and net GHG emission reductions or removals will be achieved.
ccb-5273:
Bosques Cautin is a medium sized forestry company in Chile, operating managed planted forests with the aim of supplying primary forest products in the domestic and international markets. Now the company is expanding the scope of its operations to include social, environmental and particularly climate change variables by transforming part of its commercial stands in protected forest to enhance carbon sinks.
This is a grouped project whose development encompasses simultaneously the application of the CCB Version 3.0 Standard and the VCS Version 4.6 Standard, VM0010 Methodology; Sectoral scope 14: AFOLU; Project category: IFM; Project activity type: Conversion of Logged to Protected Forest Project. The project is developed in 8,078 acres of planted forests made up by Eucalyptus globulus, Eucalyptus nitens and Radiata pine stands. The project will be developed in two stages, in Stage 1; 3,647 acres will be incorporated to the project and in Stage 2; 4,431 acres where IFM practices are expected to occur as a result of project activities.
The project is expected to capture over 6.5 million tCO2e when fully implemented. A preliminary estimate of the annual average and total reductions and removals are for Stage 1 of 3,158,040 tCO2e in a 40 years period with an average annual reduction of 78,951 tCO2e.
From the social point of view, it will impact nearly 200 community members for whom their livelihood will be improved with better education, improved connectivity and small business opportunities. From the environmental perspective, positive change in biodiversity is expected as improved conservation of high value conservation areas and in a buffer, area made up by native forests of 3,867 acres.
The company business as usual activities in the remainder of the forest estate will continue and will assure its permanence. The provisional additionality analysis demonstrates that the proposed project activity is economically (or financially) less attractive than the current land use.
ccb-5283:
The Seram Climate and Conservation (SERCOVA) project is an Improved Forest Management (IFM) project that converts logging activities into protected forest activities. SERCOVA is being implemented on a concession area under a forestry license holds by a company named PT Strata Pacific. 
The total size of PT Strata Pacific concession is 73,365 ha, consisting of a total 5,880 ha for protection area, 2,009 for non-effective area, and 66,076 ha for the effective area (i.e. Primary Forest, Secondary Forest, and Non-Forest). The eligible area for Improved Forest Management (IFM) is 56,189 (i.e. Primary Forest and Secondary Forest). The overall methodology for calculating emissions and removals/reductions is using the Verified Carbon Standard (VCS) VM0010 methodology for IFM. This methodology is applicable because the project activity includes planned timber harvest, and under the project scenario, forest use is limited to activities that do not result in commercial timber harvest or forest degradation. The selected carbon pools were the above ground biomass, deadwood, and harvested wood products.
